The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions. Our findings reveal that, while loop topological features may cause minor numerical discrepancies among closely spaced values of the Mandelstam variable, this issue can be negligible for function evaluations. The variation in gravitational potential in solids gives rise to transverse energy currents similar to electric currents generated by gravity's direction. The non-equilibrium situation in solids is thus comparable to the equilibrium state in quantum black-body thermodynamics. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities. 
In particular, Delegated RingCT is designed to address a major DPoS-based cryptocurrency platform, providing its users with anonymous and stealth transaction capabilities. 
As such, Delected RingCT can be considered a suitable solution for enhancing the anonymity and privacy of this and other DPoS-based cryptocurrencies. 
Our Delegated RingCT software implementation is now freely accessible under the permissive BSD License at GitHub, provided in full on the above-mentioned site. 
All associated benchmarking test data is available on Bitbucket. 
In addition to Delegated RingCT, this research also demonstrates the adaptability of Delegated Proof of Stake with other advanced cryptographic protocols, including Delegated Zero-Knowledge Proofs and Delegated RingCT, resulting in a potentially significant advancement in the field of cryptocurrency privacy and anonymity. 
In particular, Delegated RingCT offers a compatible and efficient solution for enhancing the anonymity and privacy of DPoS-based cryptocurrencies, such as Delegated RingCT for Bitcoin, while other comparable ZKProof and RCT implementations may also be eligible for similar consideration. 
In the future, this research proposes the exploration of a broader class of cryptographic protocols compatible with DPoS, where Delegated RingCT may serve as a suitable prototype for developing and testing consensus mechanisms that integrate high levels of anonymity and privacy with efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrencies. 
In essence, Delegated RingCT represents a suitable exemplar for investigating the development of other cryptographic protocols and features that integrate high levels of anonymity and privacy with efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrencies. 
In the long term, this research proposes the exploration of a broader class of cryptocurrency with anonymous and private transactions, as well as a scalable and efficient decentralised cryptocurrency.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can be applied to various mechanics predictions without prior knowledge, thus enabling new model and data contributions. Moreover, the method successfully integrated existing models and adapted them for novel use cases, showcasing its effectiveness through reduced errors in mechanics predictions. The method's potential was validated by successfully integrating it into a solid-section classification problem, where it successfully transferred existing knowledge from 2D to 3D classifications and demonstrated superior performance with fewer training iterations. This occurred at the cost of minimal performance in the initial 2D classification task due to the inevitable trade-off in the proposed approach. The research offers a promising outlook for continual learning in the mechanics community and hints at novel strategies for cooperative learning within the field. The results presented can be replicated by applying the method to diverse mechanics predictions, such as damage analysis and material design. The research offers a groundbreaking approach to cooperative learning, opening up fresh avenues in the mechanics community. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. In this paper, we investigate the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Our findings reveal that a pretraining corpus composed of formal texts enhances the model's ability to learn in-context, especially when dealing with informal texts. Conversely, a pretraining corpus of informal texts is less effective when the model is trained on a different set of informal texts. Additionally, our few-shot learning assessment confirms the model's dependence on the pretraining corpus origin. In terms of corpus size, we find that a larger pretraining corpus contributes to better in-context learning, although the rate of improvement lessens as the corpus grows. A key insight from our research is that in-context learning can sometimes underperform fine-tuning when using a small dataset; thus, a larger pretraining corpus can boost the model's performance in such scenarios. In contrast, a pretraining corpus of 700M tokens is insufficient for in-context learning to surpass fine-tuning when dealing with a larger 22GB dataset. In light of these findings, our analysis suggests various applications for in-context learning, including reducing computation costs, balancing data shortages with limited resources, and prioritizing specific knowledge sources (e.g., domain-specific or formal texts). Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of considering both the origin and size of a pretraining corpus when using LLMs for in-context learning. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources across layers of the network. Leveraging techniques such as blockchain, virtual reality, and predictive analytics, we can enable seamless and efficient management of MNs. However, the effectiveness of these units for vision-and-language synthesis tasks has not been explored until now. In our study, we utilized acoustic units called monophones and derived zero-speech synthesis systems for speech synthesis in languages where monophonic transcription data are available. Our experiment revealed that a zero-speech synthesis system based on monophones outperformed the existing system based on suprasegments, particularly in terms of speech naturalness. Additionally, the monophone-based system demonstrated advantages in terms of task completion and overall performance in the MashupATTS dataset. Therefore, the monophone can be considered a more suitable acoustic unit for zero-speech synthesis applications. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across earlier stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. This criterion enables the identification of valuable resources within any quantum system and reveals previously unrecognized resources in existing models.
This analysis led to the discovery of probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum correlations that can efficiently convert bipolar qubits into a universally valuable resource, typically referred to as quantum entanglement.
This breakthrough demonstrates that the traditionally restricted concept of entanglement can be replaced with less restrictive correlations in specific scenarios while retaining its valuable properties.
This research was applied to the analysis of resource transfer between different parties in several quantum communication protocols, resulting in newly devised probabilistic techniques.
This led to the development of a new method for determining lower bounds on the success probability of these resource transfer protocols.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques. Additionally, we observed the occurrence of a superlattice of resonant frequencies in the horizontal plane excitation case. Finally, we conducted a stability analysis of the completed system, consisting of a cup filled with an unbounded Newtonian fluid, by accounting for the fluid's conservation laws through a Lagrangian formalism adapted from the material line description. This approach allowed us to derive the intrinsic curvature of the fluid's free surface boundary due to its transport. With these factors taken into consideration, we performed stable periods analysis through numerical integration of the reconstructed system dynamics. The results showed notable differences in the dynamic behavior of this system compared to the lumped model alone. With the exact conservation laws from the material line formalism applied, we were able to derive an equation governing the cup's center of mass dynamics in periodic motion, influencing its coupling with the pendulum motion. Furthermore, we demonstrated the stability and uniqueness of steady-state solutions for the completed system through a combination of analytical and numerical methods. These findings provide a framework for observing an extraordinary dynamic behavior - a stable, long-lasting pendulum motion - emerging from the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee. Our analysis confirms that this remarkable phenomenon can be attributed to a combination of excitations and the fluid's behavior during periodic motion. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of the dynamic behavior of fluids in SISI dynamics and bridges this knowledge with the observed stable pendulum motion phenomenon. Additionally, we identified key factors - the fluid's transport and the pivot position's variability - that significantly impact the dynamic behavior of the system. Our results demonstrate the unique dynamics and stability characteristics of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion. These findings can be utilized to model other types of dynamical boundary value problems more effectively. This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of errors, and applying nonlinear control techniques to maintain this safety under performance constraints. Due to the infeasibility of directly optimizing the PSA, the problem is reformulated as an optimal control task with a finite horizon, with the optimizer's trajectory tending towards a safe and optimal equilibrium. Through this reformulation, it is demonstrated that the system's trajectory can reach a safe and optimal equilibrium, and the associated safety and optimality conditions are analyzed. A key finding shows that the BCFB and BPC algorithms are effective in achieving this safe and optimal equilibrium, and the study includes a numerical example to illustrate these findings. Finally, the study explores how the proposed theories can be applied to a braked electric bicycle in the presence of errors. Experimental outcomes confirm the system's ability to safely converge to an optimal equilibrium while performing challenging tasks. Additionally, it is observed that BPC leads to faster convergence and similar safety properties as BCFB. Finally, the system's safety and optimality properties under performance constraints are unaffected by errors. In the specific context of the braked electric bicycle, the threshold error values were found to be 5% for BPC and 10% for BCFB. Nonetheless, these errors result in a notable loss of performance capabilities, indicating the need for more efficient approaches to tackle this problem in the future. A potential solution could be the incorporation of a learning mechanism within the system, enabling it to adapt control strategies to various external influences in the future. A brief overview of a promising potential architecture for this type of system is also presented. Ultimately, the main conclusion of this study is that the proposed theories provide a solid foundation for optimizing the trade-off between performance and safety in the presence of errors for a specific category of nonlinear systems. This is achieved through the implementation of nonlinear control techniques that can safely and efficiently converge to an optimal equilibrium under performance constraints. A key aspect of these theories is the innovative use of a performance safety assessment metric that facilitates the analysis of system safety in the presence of errors, and the optimization of its trajectory to ensure safe and efficient operation. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to each other, as well as in relation to the first-principle theory it originates from. The research demonstrates that the dipole-based model surpasses the velocity-based model in terms of accuracy, particularly in scenarios where high-frequency interactions occur. Conversely, the velocity-based model yields precise results in situations characterized by slow frequency changes. We introduce a general framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome the complex alignment and correspondence-finding issue. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features a suite of innovative components, including a generalizable keypoint detector, a correspondence finder that generates multiple correspondence options due to partial occlusions, and a keypoint-based matcher that weighs incoming points based on their similarity to reference keypoints. Additionally, we propose a novel keypoint-based alignment method that maintains network stability and generalizability by switching to iterative Closest Point (ICP) after a certain number of training steps. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark. Furthermore, our calculations for $D^*$ and $D^*_s reveal a notable difference in their distribution amplitudes, primarily due to the charmed quark's large mass. Additionally, we derive distribution amplitudes for the $\phi$ meson, finding its longitudinal distribution to be predominantly driven by the strange quarks' momentum, a phenomenon also observed in the vector kaon. Lastly, the distribution amplitudes of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ exhibit distinct variations. In addressing the methodological intricacies of these calculations, we also derive analytical parameters for the light-front wave functions of the mesons and provide a comparison of our findings with other studies. Moreover, our research allows for a estimation of the extraction of parton distribution functions at very low $x$ through QCD evolution. In line with recent studies using the quark-spiral model, our results indicate the feasibility of obtaining parton distribution functions at very low $x$ using QCD evolution. In conclusion, the present study is an initial calculation aimed at promoting the use of light-front distribution amplitudes for momentum-sharing analysis among mesons. Our proposed algorithm leverages the capabilities of a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to predict future features and actions in videos. By using the RNN to generate future features, we can then use various action recognition techniques to identify the corresponding actions. Testing our approach on the challenging HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets, our results demonstrate the unique advantages of our method in anticipating future features and actions. Specifically, our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on these datasets by accurately predicting features and actions 10% and 5% more often, respectively. Furthermore, our algorithm exhibits reduced timing constraints while maintaining high accuracy, making it notably faster than other predictors. We refer to our method as the RNN-based Future Feature-based Action Prediction algorithm, or RNN-FFAP for short. Given its exceptional performance, we believe RNN-FFAP has the potential to be used in various applications in feature and action prediction. The code for RNN-FFAP can be found on our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/samhpcarson/RNN-FFAP. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for multiple types of 3D transformations including scaling, rotation, and translation. TPC achieves this through two main components: a novel set of simplified models that perform well in specific transformation categories and a reliable method for validating certificate integrity. Experimental results have demonstrated that TPC significantly improves robustness compared to state-of-the-art point cloud models, with superior performance on multiple datasets including global and indoor applications such as S3P and S3I. Notably, our approach is the first to offer security assurances at stretchable distances and has particular importance in applications requiring reliable long-range navigation. In addition to point cloud models, our code also supports integration with the popular MPA framework, making it easily accessible for implementation. A formal description of our work can be found in the accompanying paper, with full codes and an integrity-checked repository available at https://github.com/atsireesha/TPC. We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22. 
This work further incorporates and extends the rational T-equivariant cohomology computation previously defined in Br22 in the rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology context. 
This research also shows that the resulting T-equivariant cohomology computation is compatible with both the T^2-equivariant theory of Gre05, and the minimal T-equivariant theory of Bar22. 
This paper also presents multiple case studies validating the resulting computation, and examines its consequences in these specific contexts. 
These specific cases were found to be consistent with either prior existing mathematical theories, such as the theory of Breuckmann19, or later developed theories such as the 'T-equivariant Lecithin Lamp postulate' introduced in Br22. 
This research particularly found an interesting geometric relationship between the rational T-equivariant cohomology of CP(V), and the generation of complex lines in the projective space. 
Ultimately, this research provides a valuable extension and integration of the 'T-equivariant Lecithin Lamp postulate' into the context of rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology, and develops its corresponding 'elliptic extension'.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized model based on a half-space foundation was used to investigate the acoustic effects of impact that reach the listener's ears. An analytical expression was developed to describe the sound waveform, and numerical simulations were conducted using a point mass and a cone-frustum impacter to test its validity. The results showed that the sound's perceptibility is influenced by four factors: the stiffness, density, Poisson's ratio, and loss factor of the ground material. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for classical mathematics. This approach resonates with the majority of scholarly views, such as those of Heine, Bertrand Russell, and Fraisse. Furthermore, our investigation confirms that the infinitesimal method of Berkeley and Mandelbrode, which is often considered innovative, in fact complies with the rules of Leibnizian calculus as defined by Robinson. Lastly, an attempt to distance Leibniz from the infinitesimal method due to its supposed disagreement with the Weierstrassian formulation is unwarranted, as this method can be derived logically from the axiomatic system of Robinson. In contrast, Leibniz's reservations towards the method were grounded in his metaphysical concerns, which often led him to reject mathematical concepts deemed 'absurd'. This metaphysical Leibniz is often overlooked in modern scholarship, such as by Ishiguro and Levey. In conclusion, the most faithful representation of Leibnizian calculus continues to be the axiomatic framework of Robinson, which can satisfactorily address all criticisms leveled against the infinitesimal method. Moreover, even if one chooses to adopt a Weierstrassian or Arthurian formulation, the method of Berkeley and Mandelbrode remains compatible with the original Leibnizian calculus as defined by Robinson. Lastly, Leibniz's rejection of the infinitesimal method should be attributed to his metaphysical rather than mathematical misconceptions. In this spirit, a renewed metaphysics could help to revitalise the method, making it an invaluable tool for modern mathematics.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. Bosonic dark matter, modeled as ultralight waves or waves near their Compton frequency, can be detected through ground-based experiments examining their gravitational effects on materials. Current experiments primarily rely on analyzing low-frequency segments of sensors' output signals, up to 10 Hz, using time-series analysis. We've developed a method to detect these signals using machine learning and have successfully applied it to actual data from a detector measuring gravitational effects of bosonic dark matter on a cryogenic setup. This setup consists of three cryogenic detectors placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle in a sealed canister and is part of the NIBIN experiment. We've taken actual measurements and combined them with mathematical models to train a machine learning algorithm, achieving accurate results by integrating signals within a broader frequency band, up to 0.1 Hz, in a way that minimizes noise from other sources. This approach may improve experiments' ability to find these low-frequency signals and could be applied broadly to other ground-based experiments. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines upper and lower bounds for Kc. The study also provides examples of one-dimensional Radon measure inversion problems that yield Dirac composite measures, in addition to investigating the infinite-dimensional case under the constraint of bounded total variation. The latter problem leads to characterizing the total variation bounded BPC solution set in terms of the basis pursuit in the discrete (BPD) solution set with a soft-thresholding approach at Kc. The paper further extends these inverse problems to higher-dimensional Radon measures on torus dimensions d greater than or equal to 2. The results show that even in the d = 2 case, the formulation of BPC yields novel methods for recovering Radon measures while demonstrating the limitations of its low-frequency and basis-pursuit approaches. The study concludes by highlighting its contributions and potential applications, including its potential for extending these results to the recovery of functions rather than measures. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the V1Model architecture converts P4 programs into switch configuration code, but its current version has a major restriction: it only allows network traffic to be sent from specific input ports. This limitation prevents the network from receiving data from other ports, restricting its applications. A new compiler version has been developed that removes this restriction, allowing data to be sent and received from all ports. By using hardware features specific to the V1Model architecture, this compiler can recognize and translate specific P4 constructs into efficient switch configuration code, enabling greater parallelism and efficiency. Performance tests show that the new compiler has the same level of efficiency as the original compiler but can improve hardware usage, especially in complex P4 programs. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, we argue that a more suitable approach would be to directly solve for a function space of higher order than needed for the scalar variables. This strategy, which we will detail, enables us to work with a single, high-order function space when solving the vector transport equation, even in complex scenarios with non-straight grids. Our approach is particularly relevant in simulations involving elastic solids and multi-phase flows, where the vector transport equation plays a crucial role. We further establish that the proposed method is conservative and consistent, and even offers enhanced stability when using the lowest-order quadrature rules. To validate its effectiveness, we provide concrete numerical examples that demonstrate the performance of this new strategy in solving the vector transport equation. These numerical experiments showcase the advantages of the method, including reduced oscillations and smoother results, especially when using the lowest-order quadrature rules. Additionally, we reveal that using the Raviart-Thomas elements for the vector-valued variable is equivalent to solving for the correct function space when using the lowest-order quadrature rules. Furthermore, we derive an error estimate of the order O(h^(2 epsilon)) for approximating the curl of a linear polynomial, which serves as a benchmark solution. Based on these findings, we are confident that the proposed method will prove beneficial in a range of applications involving fluid dynamics, including solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, computing vorticity and strain from the velocity, and determining the flow direction and speed. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. A key aspect that distinguishes HBVMs from other methods is their ability to be defined both explicitly and implicitly, with the explicit form maintaining its energy-conserving properties, even in cases where the problem's differential equations are of high order. When applied to problems with constraints, implicit HBVMs can be reformulated as a flow on manifold technique, maintaining a direct connection between the differential equations, the flow, and the energy-momentum map. Our analysis shows that even when the stage equations become singular, the method remains energy-preserving. To illustrate these findings, several numerical examples are provided. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. Experimental results show that this method outperforms traditional model-parallel training with high accuracy. Specifically, it offers a faster convergence rate, reduces the memory requirement by 50%, and makes the training more stable. Moreover, it offers computational efficiency improvements of 1.9 times and 2.3 times for ResNet50 and MobileNetV2, respectively, when comparing local critic training to model-parallel training on up to 8 GPUs. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. The key advantages of our approach include its ability to be used without synchronization, its ability to process layer groups in parallel, its ability to process these groups independently, its reduced memory requirement, its computational efficiency improvements, its stable training, and its ability to facilitate structural optimization. The method is versatile and can be applied to various neural network structures, including CNNs, RNNs, and their combinations, without any modification. Furthermore, it is independent of the parameter size and communication cost, making it a reliable choice. We have conducted comprehensive experiments on image classification, language modeling, object detection, and visual question answering tasks using local critic training with positive results. The performance improvements of our approach over model-parallel training are based on the following results: a 1.9 times speedup for ResNet50, a 2.3 times speedup for MobileNetV2, a 2 times speedup for MobileNetV2 with quantization, a 2 times speedup for RNN-based language modeling, and memory requirements reduced by 50%. As a result, the system's chaotic scattering characteristics are substantially altered, facilitating the detection of intricate chameleon scattering patterns. Additionally, this article will emphasize how the ionization process can be utilized for the development of new cosmological tools, contributing to ongoing discussions about the universe's future. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. Compared to alternative estimators, NS-based estimates outperformed significantly in terms of accuracy, particularly in the latter two cases. Unlike self-driving cars and robots, bio-robots and animal locomotion simulations focus on controlling movement while maintaining stability, with key applications in fields like robotics and biology. We developed a novel approach to generate realistic locomotion paths for animals using their natural gaits, while maintaining stability and adapting to their surroundings. Our innovative method combines a 3D environment with a unique projection technique that simplifies complex calculations. Additionally, we designed a set of adjustable parameters that affect how easily animals can turn while moving, which finds practical use in animal locomotion simulations. Our theoretical framework has practical applications in fields like robotics, biology, and video game development. We tested our approach through a series of experiments using a projection-based 3D navigation system that allows multiple robots to work together in a shared environment. Our experimental results confirm that our method produces realistic and efficient locomotion paths that easily generalize to new situations. The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality and efficiency. 
Additionally, we identified the potential for future quantum hardware to excel over current classical competition. 
As such, we are making our code available to facilitate further research into quantum optimization applications.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physical laws and system dynamics from measurement data. However, a thorough analysis reveals that it is impractical to develop universal physical laws through ML and AI, given the constraints of finite measurement data and the inherent uncertainties involved. Further, an attempt to use ML and AI in this manner can result in flawed predictions that violate fundamental principles of physics, such as causality and conservation of energy. A likely outcome of this endeavor is the formulation of invalid mathematical models that are overly flexible and data-specific. In light of these limitations, we propose a more effective strategy for using ML and AI to identify physical systems, one that acknowledges the partial nature of the models it develops. By recognizing the uncertainties involved, this approach can provide valuable partial models that prioritize practical applicability over theoretical completeness. A key aspect of this method is the partial model for measurement uncertainty, proposed here, which helps to mitigate the fluctuations observed in measurement data by quantifying the uncertainty associated with the extraction of system properties from data. In the context of system dynamics, this uncertainty is reflected as fluctuations in solution trajectories, represented using a partial model that can inform partial differential equations (PDEs) through Bayesian learning. In order to illustrate these concepts, we apply the proposed partial model framework to the example of ground transportation dynamics. Although this example involves lengthy and complex mathematical derivations, the resulting partial model demonstrates a notable improvement in quantifying measurement uncertainty involved in forecasting dynamics. Ultimately, this work aims to guide researchers in using ML and AI to identify physical systems by acknowledging and addressing the associated measurement uncertainties involved. By doing so, we can develop accurate and valid partial models for the dynamics of physical systems. More information about the methods and can be found at https://indcoarse.github.io/pmm/. All related code can be accessed at https://github.com/indcoarse/pmm.ystate. Any inquiries regarding this work can be directed to sashank.srinivas@gmail.com.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and the effective elimination of obstacles from the top surface. However, we also identified a limitation of our framework in modeling the source efficiency and sought to address this issue for potential applications. We compared our results with previous studies on a single-photon source, demonstrating the significance of accounting for the waveguide input impedance in achieving high efficiency. Moreover, we explored the potential of modulating the source efficiency of the device by altering the SiO$_2$ upper cladding using nano-squaring techniques, which can reduce loss and enhance the Purcell factor. Our investigation highlighted the importance of combining advanced semiconductor fabrication techniques with cutting-edge photonic engineering to achieve single-photon emission with high efficiency. We believe our study has pivotal implications for the development of the single-photon source in quantum information processing and cryptography applications. For example, the ability to enhance the source efficiency by a factor of two through nano-squaring technology could be beneficial in the production of quantum chips on a large scale. Furthermore, the integration of the single-photon source with other quantum devices such as nanowires, quantum dots, and cavities is another area that needs to be explored in depth. Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of attributes contributing to solution diversity. Our research demonstrates that promoting diversity through fitness or attribute correlations can be ineffective and may lead to false positives, whereas attributing diversity to latent factors can be misleading due to the lack of interpretability. Consequently, we recommend using historical solution data to define attributes, thereby ensuring transparency and reliability in guiding the optimization of diverse solutions. Our approach is validated through a series of experiments using the ant problem as a test case. Additionally, our integration of this method into a lightweight evolutionary algorithm allows for efficient and diverse exploration of solution spaces. Our comparison with a range of established optimization techniques confirms that this approach yields superior diversity while requiring reduced computational resources. Our research includes all necessary code to replicate our findings, which can be accessed on our GitHub repository. https://github.com/sam-sparrow/quality-diversity.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete, even when using limited binary valuations. However, under the condition of binary and symmetric valuations, we found that a stable matching will always exist and can be found within polynomial time. Additionally, we looked at finding the best stable matches that maximise total happiness when using binary and symmetric valuations. While finding the absolute optimum is a complex problem, we identified a more practical solution for approximating it closely. The study also involved investigating how these findings relate to the groups' geometric positions, represented by three-dimensional space coordinates, yielding instances of hardness and a related, but solvable, variant. The analysis was also extended to involve small groups of size four, demonstrating the solvability and approximability in this case. The study then shifted to considering large groups of agents in three-dimensional space and assigned valuations based on their relative positions, resulting in solvability and approximability in this case as well. The paper also discusses how these results compare to other related problems. The study leads to the introduction of a new algorithmic problem, Oriented Colorful Rendezvous, and explores its feasibility on single and multi-agent variants. The challenge in this problem involves finding three-dimensional positions for a set of agents such that each pair is positioned in relation to each other as specified in their individual preference lists. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing minimal subspaces that are preserved under the Gromov--Hausdorff distance. We investigate the properties of clouds, particularly those that are stable under approximations and divide the stable clouds into two categories, being either completely isolated or infinitely dense. We focus primarily on the first category, consisting of dense subspaces that are independently closed, and determine the limits of its infinitesimal dense subspaces, resulting in expanded metric spaces with altered metrics. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for applications like radar and communication systems. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results. A pair of these antennas was also tested in a diverging array configuration to evaluate their performance when used in a diverging array setup at a fixed frequency of 36 GHz. The array's input impedance matched well with the simulated results, and the observed far-field radiation pattern exhibited a wide horizontal coverage of 140 degrees, minimal front-to-back ratio of 5.4 dB, and a wide vertical beamwidth of 20-30 degrees. The measured peak gain of the array was approximately 8.2 dBi, aligning with expected gains in mm-wave array antennas. The observed gain was also observed to decrease slightly with increased horizontal angle due to the nature of the array's geometry. The design of these microstrip patch antennas and their potential application in array forms can greatly improve gain while maintaining wide beamwidths by optimizing the array geometry for specific applications. Moreover, the simple integrated structure of these microstrip patch antennas makes them highly suitable for various applications, including phased array radar and diverging array communications. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. These decoders perform nearly as well as state-of-the-art markov based methods while using significantly less computational power, and we anticipate they will have a significant impact on the field of quantum computing, particularly in hybrid quantum classical algorithms. Moreover, the framework of agents interacting in a code environment allows us to explore new topics in fault-tolerant learning, such as the concept of code complexity, which we use to evaluate the efficacy of our decoders. This research represents the first steps towards a future of learning fault-tolerant algorithms within a quantum computing environment. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability. The quantum states produced by the system are examined and the conditions for achieving precision are identified. The study demonstrates the feasibility of using quantum jump metrology in multi-cavity systems, offering a beneficial trade-off between precision and the complexity of the quantum state. The research may open the door for the utilization of quantum jump metrology in the analysis of complex optical networks. The method employs quantum feedback from laser pulses to induce desired correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback, overcoming limitations of prior research including state complexity and practical challenges. The development of quantum jump metrology into a practical tool for measuring optical phases relies on the identification of quantum states produced by the system and pinpointing the parameters influencing precision. The study's findings can be applied to multi-cavity systems, and the results can be extended for use as reference points in the measurement of quantum mechanical phase. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions based on the quantum circuit architecture. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and gate precision, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any size is a chain with an odd number of qubits. Our research also finds that digital-analog simulation can achieve a level of accuracy for fermionic interactions that is equivalent to 10^-4 with 121 qubits, surpassing the capabilities of classical computers in this realm. Ultimately, our study highlights the potential for digital-analog quantum computing to accurately model fermionic systems at a large scale. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This approach can be viewed as initializing the networks with an overconfident feature set, similar to max-value classifying, within the scope of a probabilistic generalization framework. Consequently, our method achieves significant improvements in handling OoD scenarios without relying on unreliable posterior regularization.

Notably, our approach yields exceptional results when combined with uncertainty-based methods in various benchmarks, ultimately leading to a 9.7% improvement in the specific case of Conceptual Visual Recognition. Moreover, it offers a beneficial side effect of accelerating the optimizer, resulting in the model being more robust to adversarial attacks and data corruption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In contrast, our study focuses on CMOS sensors built with high-resistivity Czochralski wafers, allowing the full utilization of sensor active areas. In-depth analysis revealed that high-resistivity substrates pose significant challenges but also provide opportunities for enhanced functionality and sensitivity. In this study, we investigate the properties of high-resistivity substrates using experimental data and simulations. Notably, we discovered that small-scale p-ionization clouds can induce substantial noise and reduce particle detection efficiency, while large-scale clouds can persist for hundreds of ns and attenuate signal charge. Despite these obstacles, we successfully developed a method to boost particle detection rates by two orders of magnitude. Our findings suggest that using high-resistivity Czochralski substrates offers improved detection efficiency, albeit with added complexity. As detector design becomes increasingly optimized, incorporating high-resistivity substrates into monolithic CMOS sensors becomes an attractive option. Moreover, the findings emphasize the significance of accurately understanding background conditions and measurement precision for the successful realization of sterile neutrino research at DUNE. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated its accuracy by comparing it to exact solution values. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of particle transport in a turbulent flow, comparing its results to those from standard models. Our tests revealed that the standard method leads to particle collisions occurring earlier than they would in real-world conditions, resulting in increased collision rates and altered turbulence characteristics. Our algorithm, on the other hand, more accurately simulates the physical timing of particle collisions without excessive demands on computational time. Our analysis focuses on a combination of both lab-scale and real-world applications of liquid jet dynamics. This topic is significant not only because of its relevance to understanding complex fluid dynamics but also due to its implications in the field of fluid dynamics research. Furthermore, the underlying principles of fluid dynamics that we employ to understand the behavior of a liquid jet can also be applied to understanding the penetration of a solid object through the surface of a fluid. This knowledge has practical applications in various industries such as aerospace, defense, and engineering industries. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale. By treating topics as both hierarchical and granular constituents, HDTM successfully captures salient features at multiple levels, and our experiments, covering both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we validate HDTM's accuracy by evaluating its performance in two critical use cases: 1) categorizing documents based on the predicted topics and 2) transferring knowledge across domains. Given its robust capabilities, HDTM has the potential to greatly impact our understanding of large information networks and is now available as an open-source system. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. Both findings support the flux-based three-body statistical framework, and our measurements of absorptivity and lifetime distributions provide valuable resources for further testing and validation of statistical models. These results have practical applications in various areas, including the study of exoplanetary dynamics, the dynamics of star clusters, and the analysis of gravitational-wave events. Based on these findings, we also provide enhanced statistical models that can be utilized in the analysis of future gravitational-wave detectors, including improved approximations for the distribution of lifetimes and the relationship between absorptivity and binary energy, which can be expressed through a universal polynomial equation. In particular, for the case with equal masses, the absorptivity can be expressed as a quadratic function of binary energy that depends on the eccentricity, in agreement with a previously proposed model. Additionally, our analysis suggests that the distribution of lifetimes can be accurately described by a single-parameter distribution for a wide range of binary eccentricities, which can be determined through an analytically calculated expression based on the flux-based statistical framework. This simplified model of the distribution of lifetimes offers considerable computational benefits for the integration of statistical models in the analysis of future gravitational-wave detectors. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that the integration of these statistical models can significantly improve the detection confidence of gravitational-wave sources, facilitating a higher cross-detection efficiency between LIGO and other future gravitational-wave detectors. It is anticipated that these statistical models will be useful for the interpretation of future low signal-to-noise ratio detections across a range of detectors including LIGO, VIRTI-AL, and the proposed space-based missions LISA and TiDE. These models may also find applications in various astrophysical contexts including the dynamics of star clusters, exoplanetary dynamics, and the analysis of other multi-body gravitational interactions. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we introduce a subobject classifier within this category and employ it to define a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects. 
Finally, we show that the original hyperdoctrine representing predicates in continuous logic can be incorporated into this new hyperdoctrine of subobjects by restricting its domain to equivalence relations, thus mapping predicates to subobjects. 
This result allows the application of hyperdoctrine methods to investigate properties of predicates in continuous logic and relates these to subobjects within the category of topological structures. 
As an initial exploration of this capability, we determine the representable subobjects within this category, characterizing them as those for which the corresponding uniform subspaces are closed under the intersection of arbitrary arithmetical families. 
This characterization generalizes a result obtained by L. Newton in the finite case. 
Additionally, we define and study the properties of an equivalence relation representing the subobject representing universal sentences in continuous logic. 
This analysis leads to an interpretation of these sentences within the category of topological structures, revealing among other things that the sentence 'any nonempty complete metric space contains an injective mapping into any other such space' is not a theorem of continuous logic. 
This result is contrasted with the fact that this sentence is a theorem of standard first-order logic. 
Our investigation of subobjects is concluded by establishing that the subobject representing a predicate can be reduced to the subobject representing its negation within the category of equivalence relations. 
This result generalizes and continuously a corresponding result obtained by N. Donaldson in the finite case.

This extension leads to an interpretation of relative definability in continuous logic in terms of the presence of a suitable natural transformation within the hyperdoctrine representing the notions of continuity and uniformity.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, we have obtained a corollary related to a type of manifold where the scalar curvature is nonnegative, building upon a previous paper by Li and Zhang. We also provide an example illustrating that the growth condition can be avoided when the scalar curvature is positive. Furthermore, we have derived a unique theorem demonstrating that the set of all solutions to a certain partial differential equation for subharmonic functions is finite-dimensional under specific conditions, without relying on a growth estimate. We confirm that the known criteria for the finiteness of harmonic functions or polynomial growth harmonic functions are optimal, while also establishing an optimal criterion for the finiteness of $p$-harmonic functions. In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional treatment is applied, charge conservation is violated in these systems, leading to incorrect results. We develop a way to correctly calculate effective charges in metals within the framework of density functional theory. Our method relies on solving the Kohn-Sham equations with a non-local potential derived from the macroscopic polarization, then utilizing the constrained density functional theory to correct occupancy violations. Our results are validated through comparison with experimental data for aluminum and sodium, with the calculated charges aligning with the experimental outcomes. Additionally, our method allows us to examine the response of metals under external electric fields, including the unusual behavior of sodium where the effective charge exceeds the elementary charge. We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description within this range. Specifically, our analysis implies that the exponentially decaying determinstic behavior observed at large scales by Guzzi et al. should also be observed at the Kolmogorov scale, the transition to turbulence dissipation range, where the randomly induced fluctuations have not yet taken over. Our predictions are confirmed by examining the simulation data of Caillol et al. and understanding the transition to turbulence through this perspective offers valuable insights. Furthermore, our study highlights the need for greater attention to be paid to the critical transition between the inertial and dissipation range and turbulence, a transition commonly referred to as the 'onset' of turbulence. By understanding the dynamics of this transition, engineers can design an array of turbulence-producing devices known as passive grid, which has various applications and can help reduce the risk of transition to turbulence in flow within different types of fluid dynamics. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a current induced by a magnetically confined electride, an electronic state born from polarization of the insulating bulk by an external magnetization. The experimental observation of this phenomenon also necessitates a revision of the definition of topological insulators, as it can coexist with other surface states. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality. We determine the conditions under which the diffusion spike occurs, requiring that the system undergoes a crisis surface map with a tangent space intersection; this condition can be satisfied even without applying external periodic modulation. When this crisis surface map meets a diffusion condition, a scaling relationship arises, leading to enhanced diffusion. Importantly, we find that this phenomenon is universal, occurring in a wide range of systems with delayed nonlinearity and can be observed experimentally. Moreover, we provide theoretical evidence that the area of the diffusion spike in parameter space increases cubically with the system size, opening up new avenues for diffusive research. Due to its generality, this phenomenon can have significant implications for fields such as biology and medicine, where systems with delayed nonlinearity play a crucial role. Furthermore, our findings also have important ramifications for delay systems in general, including those not exhibiting diffusion. By extending our analysis to systems with multiple delay periods, we obtain a method for computing diffraction patterns in these systems, providing a new level of understanding. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Furthermore, building on this achievement, we establish a proven adequacy theorem for both denotational and operational views, thereby validating a natural notion of contextual equivalence in the stochastic lambda calculus. Notably, this equivalence is robust against varying levels of probabilistic uncertainty. Consequently, we are able to derive a proven version of the free-theorems-style "f-recover" check for a stochastic version of the PCF language, as well as establish the equivalence of denotational and operational models for a stochastic version of the Curry-Howard correspondence, thereby closing another outstanding issue. Finally, we extend our results to cover a stochastic version of the Guarded Fixed Point Theory, thereby allowing us to reason about the reasoning abilities of high-level probabilistic code. Specifically, this enables us to prove that a probabilistic version of the Sauron axiom implies a conflicting principle, thereby showing the probabilistic Sauron axiom to be inconsistent when applied to the reasoning abilities of high-level probabilistic code. Specifically, this inconsistency arises when the code may evaluate to a probabilistically positive amount of time that is less than a given threshold, set to 0.06. Conversely, we observe that this threshold is below the maximum value of 0.07 established in a recent study (Almeida et al., 2020). Additionally, we note the presence of the probabilistic Sauron axiom in yet another study (Bacci et al., 2019), while its presence was previously observed in the study by Bacci et al. as well as its generalization to reason about the reasoning abilities of high-level probabilistic code as described in the study by Bacci et al. We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider. To identify these decays, the research involved reconstructing the full recoil B-meson within hadronic end products, after which the researchers computed total branching ratios by performing statistical fits on missing mass square and dipion mass in the $\rho$-meson. The calculated total branching ratios for $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair is approximately 7.1(2.1) × 10^-4, while $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair has a branching ratio of approximately 4.2(1.6) × 10^-4. Additionally, the research provides the first observation of $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and an electron-neutrino pair, with an estimated confidence level of 4.9σ, whereas no significant results were found for $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair. Further analysis also determines upper limits for nonresonant $b$-to-$d$ tree-level decays of $B^0$ into $\rho^-$ and an electron-neutrino pair and $B^+$ into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, at $<6.2(10) \times 10^-4$ and $<4(3) \times 10^-4$ respectively, with expectations based on current theoretical models. The research also discusses potential improvements in analyzing these processes using additional data from the Belle II experiment. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the traditional spectroscopy method known as infra-red difference interferometry (IRDI), which measures the difference in infra-red spectra of reflectance and transmittance. This technique has a long history of success in identifying the molecular composition of asteroids, comets, and other objects in our solar system and wide-area field spectroscopy. By leveraging photonic technology, we developed an advanced IRDI system that not only maintains the system's sensitivity but significantly improves its sensitivity and speed. The new system's high-speed data acquisition capabilities enable real-time monitoring of an object's infra-red spectra as it moves through the beam splitter, eliminating system fluctuations and improving the detection of tiny features. Furthermore, we updated the system with an enhanced signal processing approach, known as the Munro-trace technique, to maximize the sensitivity and dynamic range, effectively doubling the system's spatial resolution and bandwidth. The revised system has a 12-bit dynamic range and a 12.5 micrometer sampling period, facilitating the temporary isolation of interferometric patterns and accelerating data processing. Our innovative approaches have prepared photonic IRDI for future applications, such as deep space exploration and the Europedia mission, and have paved the way for new technologies in photonic spectroscopy and interferometry. The Europedia mission, in particular, will benefit from the revised system's enhanced sensitivity and spatial resolution, and could potentially detect biochemicals on targets up to 30 astronomical units, rather than the current limit of 20. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints to map states from one domain to their counterparts in another domain.  Moreover, it allows the learned domain mapping to be used effectively for goal achievement domains that differ from the mapping domain, and proves the method applicable across diverse domain variations, including dynamic system changes and agent design modifications.  The method is evaluated on multiple complex domains and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.  Code for this work is available at https://github.com/alexrame/ImitationAcrossDomainVariations.
