A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with existing magnetic fields. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to the initial mass function mass range, $50-100M_{\odot}$. 

These simulations show that when the magnetic field amplification is moderate to high in mass, $50-100M_{\odot}$, it significantly increases the formation of secondary protostars. Within the parameter range studied, it leads to approximately $60\%$ of stars forming protostars in multiple systems, as opposed to a rate of less than $10\%$ seen in simulations with no magnetic effects. 

The increased formation of multiple systems in these simulations means that the final mass of the primary protostar in binary systems will, on average, be less than half the total mass of the system. This reduction in primary protostar mass has implications for the minimum mass of the binary system that can be incorporated into galaxy clusters through the merger of equal-mass binaries in the early universe. 

Given that most of the initial protostars formed in these simulations have magnetic field values close to their maximum possible range, it's likely that the process of ambipolar diffusion significantly reduces the magnetic field strength in the accretion disk before the protostar is formed. This means that the increased formation of binary systems due to magnetic effects may not necessarily be reflected in the final mass of the binary system. Consequently, the typical binary system mass may still be higher than expected, primarily due to a range of unequal-mass binaries. Therefore, it would be unhelpful to use the initial mass function derived from binary systems that formed in the early universe to understand the astrophysical processes that made the first stars. 

In contrast, the increased formation of binary systems in these simulations has implications for the formation of multiple star systems. It's likely that many of these systems will eventually form open clusters in the early universe, as the process of stellar formation continues. In fact, the increased formation of binary systems due to magnetic effects may be responsible for the early formation of multiple star systems, as the process of stellar formation continues, ultimately resulting in the early universe being populated with multiple star systems.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated. In addition to establishing the existence of an equilibrium, we demonstrate the uniqueness of an equilibrium when the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls is only mildly variable. Uniqueness is further demonstrated in two specific contexts: when dependence is uniformly convex with variable coefficients and when there are uniform bounds on the controls. Uniqueness is also demonstrated in two specific contexts: when dependence is uniformly convex with variable coefficients and when there are uniform bounds on the controls. In another context, we show that an equilibrium is unique when there are uniform bounds on the controls, a result closely related to Lagrangian dependence on controls being uniformly bounded. Finally, we address the continuous time version of the problem, a subject of ongoing research.

We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release VICTOR research implementation, model weights, and dataset at https://github.com/hypothtc/victor. Additionally, a live demo is accessible at https://victor-dreamfusion.pytorch.org/. Upon visiting, users can upload their own outfit photos to instantly receive compatibility ratings and potential mismatch warnings. To produce these real-time results, VICTOR's implementation can be deployed using the PyTorch TorchServe framework, as evidenced by the live demo available at https://victor-dreamfusion.pytorch.org/. We intend to extend our research to cover multiple languages, recognizing the significance of fashion compatibility across cultural boundaries. Currently, we have only explored English as our base language, hoping to explore the potential of fashion compatibility across language and culture in future studies. To facilitate this, we will develop an advanced, multi-language Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR-MUL) that can adapt to various linguistic and cultural contexts by leveraging fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training, while being able to learn essential fashion rules from each dataset. We plan to explore VICTOR-MUL's potential in future research, but for now, we will stick with the base version, VICTOR. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of heavy and light holes in the valence bands. Consequently, a low-mass light hole type conduction is produced, resulting in higher hole mobility in comparison to the standard high-mass heavy hole type conduction. Specifically, we find that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ increases its hole mobility by a factor of two while reducing the hole mass by 85% along the compressive strain direction. Our conclusions encourage the exploration of strain engineering to boost the performance of GaN-based power electronic devices. Moreover, they open up novel opportunities for gallium nitride to be utilized in advanced quantum devices, such as spin-orbit qubits and Hall bars, by aligning the strain to create the desired quantum confinement effects. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies modify the input data by extracting temporal attributes from individual facts, effectively creating new negative samples for each fact, and hope this boosts the model's performance. A key drawback of this approach is the increased likelihood of the model overfitting, as the number of parameters grows with the number of added temporal scopes. In this research, we propose a new method for learning temporal scopes within knowledge graphs, where each scope represents a collective negative sample applicable to an entire class of similar facts. We model this as a separate graph, where each node represents a cluster of similar facts, and each edge connects two nodes sharing a common attribute, and demonstrate that learning temporal scopes within this meta-graph can enhance the embedding of the original graph, resulting in improved performance on the resultant model's testing data. This improvement can be achieved without risking the model overfitting, as the added parameters are confined to the meta-graph, and are thus independent of the original graph. We test the efficacy of our method using two datasets, one for modeling individual clusters and one for predicting when individual facts will be generated, and demonstrate that it outperforms existing methods, including those specifically designed for fact-level prediction, by up to 4% in terms of accuracy and 11% in terms of mean absolute error. A thorough evaluation of our method's effectiveness, and the potential for its application to various domains, is presented in the form of an implementation available on GitHub at the listed address. Experimental results indicating the method's superiority over existing solutions are also presented. In particular, our approach proves more effective than HBRE+ at scope-level temporal scope prediction, and for the FEAT-level temporal scope prediction, it outperforms not only HBRE+ but also RE-biLLE. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if this Bates' theorem holds universally or if there are instances where strong shift equivalence directly implies Morita equivalence. If the latter is true, it would allow us to bypass the complexities of invariant measures and approximate unitary inclusions, thus providing a more straightforward connection between these two concepts. Notably, this relationship is evident in the context of singular trees, as evidenced by a companion article. Additionally, this note offers a simplified proof of Muhly-Rourke's theorem which relates Morita equivalence to strong shift equivalence, as well as generalizations to metric graphs, whose C*-algebras may not necessarily be row-finite. Furthermore, this note explores the notion of weak shift equivalence and its associated separations, as well as its connection to 1-sparse matrices and their generated C*-algebras. Finally, this note presents an instance of strong shift equivalence that does not imply Morita equivalence, as evidenced in the context of complete bipartite graphs CN,m,N-n-m. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective tools for processing sequential data. Their ability to capture contextual and temporal relationships makes them widely applied in tasks such as natural language processing, where they are often used for classification, generation, and analysis, as well as in signal processing and astronomy for extracting features from time-series and audio data. However, traditional recurrent models suffer from a limitation in their forward propagation mechanism, leading to computationally expensive gradients and vanishing or exploding gradients during backpropagation. In an attempt to improve upon these limitations, various alternative recurrent models have been developed,, including gated, based on the incorporation of vector gates and the concept of tensor factorization. In this study, a novel framework called multi-plicative 2-dimensional (MP2D) network is proposed, where tensor factorization is used in both the contextual and temporal directions. The MP2D model is then applied to the natural language classification task in comparison with established models. The results indicate that MP2D significantly outperforms traditional recurrent models and often achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art models while offering the advantage of reduced parameters. Furthermore, MP2D demonstrates an impressive ability to visualize semantic features through the use of tensor tensor-guided feature learning, resulting in clear and intuitive features that can improve the understanding of models in deep learning. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established RE as a challenging task, with deep
neural networks performing satisfactorily. Despite these advances, deep neural networks
are hindered by their interpretation difficulties, creating concerns about their reliability
and fairness. In contrast, graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a unique advantage in RE by
representing a relationship as a graph of entity interactions. With the ability to model
long-range relationships, GNNs demonstrate particular effectiveness. A recent study,
however, has pointed out the limitations of GNNs in RE, emphasizing their sensitivity to
node degree. Based on these insights, we propose a novel Convolutional GNN (CGNN) for
RE. By employing a special 'fake' node to standardize node degree, our proposed CGNN
can effectively convolve graphs of entity interactions to extract relevant relationships. In
our experiments using the FB24 dataset, our proposed CGNN has achieved remarkable
results, surpassing state-of-the-art benchmarks. Moreover, we have also assessed the
fairness of our model using the FairVerdict framework. Interestingly, we found that our
proposed model exhibited relative fairness in comparison to the state-of-the-art deep
neural networks. With the ability to model long-range relationships, along with its
fairness and reliability, our proposed model presents a strong candidate for RE tasks. 
Additionally, we conducted a parameter reduction to verify the effectiveness of our model. 
The code used for this research can be found at the following link: 
https://github.com/damirsaric/CGNN_RE.git. 
A paper detailing our methodology is available at the following link:

To address this, we develop a novel approach of representing each component as a separate hypergraph, and combining these hypergraphs with a high-degree of overlap. This results in a complex system represented by a hypergraph series, which facilitates the application of numerical methods such as homology and percolation theory. In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe abnormalities and organs' positions relative to each other. Leveraging this
anatomical context can enhance the accuracy of learning algorithms. We therefore
define a set of rules that translate doctors' written descriptions of organs' and
abnormalities' positions into measurable coordinates, treating these coordinates as
supervisory signals. We show that these coordinates can be represented as
transformations of the relative positions of bases, where base features are learned
end-to-end. Specifically, we investigate three scenarios: 1) reporting organ positions
relative to a fixed point, 2) describing positions relative to other organs, and 3)
describing enclosures of organs. We propose the Translational Anatomical Context
(TAC) framework to incorporate these coordinates into analysis. We evaluate TAC using
data from the LiTS-EBP dataset, focusing on detecting pancreas lesions. Experimentally,
it is found that incorporating anatomical context as supervisory signals yields an
85\% improvement in Delong's test for comparing ROC curves and a $4.5\%$
improvement in the AUC. Where organs' positions are ambiguous, as in the case of
spleen positions, we find that incorporating this information as supervisory signals
yields an 11\% improvement in the AUC. Furthermore, it is observed that incorporating
anatomical context as supervisory signals increases the detection rate of pancreas
lesions by an 8%, which, when coupled with an improvement in the AUC of
$6.2\%, yield an overall $14\%$ improvement in the AUC of detecting pancreas lesions. 
Ultimately, the performance of segmentation is found to be at its maximum when the
anatomical structure is fully reconstructed. We publicly release our code for the
project on https://github.com/d-d-d/d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d_d. 
To address the issue of anatomical context ambiguity, we propose a joint estimation
of positions and structures by employing an anatomical constraint, where the relationship
between organs' positions is modelled as a geometric transformation of bases. We find
this to be effective in detecting pancreas lesions, where the structure of pancreas has
previously proven challenging to reconstruct, yielding an 10\% improvement in the AUC

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. These approximations lead to four distinct cases: (i) perturbations approaching a stability crisis, where an alternating series of two real and one imaginary solution emerges, consistent with Nyquist's argument; (ii) perturbations exceeding a stability threshold, where an exclusively real solution arises, consistent with Kelvin-Helmholtz instability; (iii) perturburations involving only imaginary solutions when an imaginary wavenumber arises, where an analogy with Airy's differential is identified; and (iv) behavior around singularities, where a series of imaginary solutions emerges, including a particular case where real solutions also occur, all consistent with d'Alembert's equation. These cases, developed via an innovative application of the Boussinesq approximation, offer insights into previously unexplored regions of stratified turbulence. Additionally, it is determined that asymptotic solutions, when connected, yield a series of connections, including a connection to the Rayleigh-Kuo criterion for instability, a connection to the Taylor dispersion theory, a connection to the Rhines scale, and, finally, a connection to the Obukhov length scale. Ultimately, this research provides a series of mathematical, physical, and historical connections to various renowned theories in geophysical sciences. However, the corresponding paper has not been formally submitted due to an imposed pre-print embargo by the corresponding author. Consequently, this pre-print is presented for public consumption at this time.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, we capture the agent's predictive model of the environment. We evaluate the agent's performance on the MatterPort3D navigation benchmark and observe a notable improvement in goal achievement rates, particularly with reduced vision. Under the assumption that the final state particles are well reconstructed, the top quark pair background can be effectively suppressed by utilizing analytical matrix element weights based on unpolarized quark and anti-quark distribution functions. We found that with these matrix element weights, the Higgs boson pair signal can be extracted from the background with less than 10% residual contamination after applying the cuts. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that the matrix element technique can achieve a better sensitivity to the Higgs boson pair production cross section with respect to the standard parton shower-based approach, while also allowing for the top quark pair background to be determined with higher accuracy using the correct unpolarized initial states. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is a promising direction. The current method involving sampling from a uniform grid does not account for solution gradient information, leading to suboptimal results. To bridge this gap, a new adaptive sampling approach is proposed, grounded in the principle of minimizing the worst-case absolute element of the Jacobian matrix's eigenvalue approximation. The effectiveness of this technique was tested on two challenging nonlinear problems, resulting in accelerated convergence and reduced required samples by two orders of magnitude for the first problem and by a factor of ten for the second, consistent with the approximate degree of freedom for these equations. The proposed method demonstrates substantial improvements to computational efficiency while efficiently navigating the complex geometric structures inherent in these problems. To access the repository, please follow the provided instructions. Further information can be obtained by contacting the corresponding author at [sven.haas@ethz.ch](sven.haas@ethz.ch).

This study examines the behavior and simulation models related to the negative capacitance effect (NCE) observed in the gate-insulator layer of ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) with a HfO2 channel. Through comparison of different models, we evaluate their capacity to predict changes in the capacitance and conductance under various voltages and temperatures. While the NCE model based on the Landau theory accurately predicts capacitance variations, it fails to predict temperature-induced shifts in the threshold voltage. Conversely, the Jaynes-Cummings-like model effectively predicts both capacitance and threshold voltage changes with temperature. Furthermore, we find that the NCE models predict a significant reduction in voltage-induced damage, with the threshold voltage requiring higher voltages to shift by a certain amount compared to models not incorporating NCE. This means the NCE can help mitigate voltage-induced damage in FeFETs. Moreover, combining the NCE with a variable relaxation time leads to a significant improvement in the device's performance, allowing for better storage of charge and reduced leakage. Specifically, we find that the total storage capacity increases by a factor of 24, the effective storage capacity increases by a factor of 57, and the decay time is extended by a factor of 7. Additionally, we find that the consideration of NCE results in a notable improvement in the conduction compared to models not incorporating NCE, allowing the device to store more charge before conductance increases. Specifically, we find that the conductance increases by a factor of 21 near the peak storage capacity and the total storage capacity increases by a factor of 26. These improvements validate the use of NCE models to enhance the performance of FeFETs. Finally, we evaluate the energy efficiency of the device, finding that the consideration of NCE results in a notable improvement in energy efficiency, allowing the device to store more information with less energy compared to models not incorporating NCE, over a range from 10^4 to 10^9 electrons. Specifically, we find that the energy efficiency increases by a factor of 21 near the peak storage capacity and the total storage capacity increases by a factor of 26. A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and identifies vulnerability propagation paths through structural analysis of the graph. By examining 1,520 libraries from the Cargo ecosystem over a 4-year period, this study reveals that Cargo libraries are predominantly susceptible to insecure memory usage, false positives, and code injection attacks. Notably, the research finds that library vulnerabilities frequently result from copied code containing known security flaws. Additionally, this study identifies multiple instances of vulnerability multiplicity, where a single library is affected by multiple security vulnerabilities, often inherited from previous versions and inherited libraries. Overall, this research highlights the need for Cargo-specific security governance strategies that can effectively manage propagation of security vulnerabilities and True positives. These can be achieved through code review, focusing on removing inherited vulnerabilities, implementing security patches, and upgrading libraries to address vulnerabilities. By targeting library maintenance, Cargo's security vulnerability propagation can be controlled, and its overall security efficacy improved. These efforts will also impact other Ecosystems, like Rust's, by promoting widespread adoption of the best security practices for Cargo. In addition to the formal analysis, this research presents practical solutions to mitigate security vulnerabilities in various libraries, contributing to both Cargo's and Rust's overall security. Additionally, this research provides visual representations of the dependency vulnerability graph and vector arithmetic operations in Cargo to help researchers and developers identify potential security vulnerabilities. Furthermore, this research recommends employing vector arithmetic operations with memory bounds checking to address insecure memory usage and improve the general security of the libraries. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational cost, with a significant reduction in model complexity. Specifically, our OCNs achieved an 89.60% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet ILSVRC 2012 challenge, with an extremely low error rate compared to other orientation-robust models. Our proposed orientation convolutional neural network has great potential for application in various robust image recognition tasks. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN via KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively. Additionally, we developed a novel procedure to evaluate the relatedness of trigger images, which could also benefit the development of customized Trojan patterns based on image embeddings. Our code will be publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hunkoff/TyGAT. Our evaluation results can be found on our website at https://www.hunkoff.com/TyGAT.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. By simulating the planetary formation and evolution process, we identified the expected abundance of volatile elements like carbon and nitrogen in exoplanet mantles and cratonic layers. Our model indicates that the carbon and nitrogen abundances in these layers are substantially lower than in the corresponding stars, ranging from 15% to 500% less. The key devolatilisation process responsible for this occurs during the accretion of planetesimals from a protoplanetary disk with a short duration, typically less than 2 million years. Our model also demonstrates the correlation between devolatilisation and the mass of the disk's massive objects, with lesser devolatilisation occurring in planets forming from disks with multiple massive objects. The devolatilisation of carbon and nitrogen in terrestrial exoplanets has a notable impact on estimating the habitability of these planets due to the key roles these elements play in biological and geochemical processes. Consequently, taking devolatilisation into consideration may lead to the discovery of Earth-like planets with reduced habitability potential. Conversely, employing model with reduced devolatilisation yields better agreement with constraints from seismology and geochemistry on the habitability of exoplanet K2-18b. Our research contributes novel insights into the chemical structure of terrestrial exoplanets informed by devolatilisation processes, paving the way for improved accurate estimates of planetary habitability. Additionally, our model generates testable predictions regarding planetary internal structures, which could be verified through future planetary interior modeling and analysis of planetary orbits. Furthermore, devolatilisation influences the abundance of carbon and nitrogen in exoplanet crusts, which could be compared to the orbital periods of the planets through spectral analysis of the host stars. The devolatilisation processes in star composition also impact planetary sizes, which could be examined by comparing the orbital periods and planet sizes with other exoplanets in the study sample. Our model indicates that devolatilisation results in smaller sizes for planets orbiting closer to their host stars, which could be verified through future research. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. Moreover, the proposed method will allow us to define a universal mathematical structure for modal logic as a whole, encompassing all individual modal logics within it. By extending our approach to include other deductive systems, we will show how to generalize the method to handle a broad range of other logics as well. Using this categorical method, we will study fundamental properties of modal logic truths and related algebraic and topological characteristics. Lastly, the method will enable us to explore potential applications in computer science, particularly in the areas of program semantics, logic programming, and automated reasoning. Specifically, we will focus on examining the essential features of modal logic-based logics in the context of program semantics and search logic in the context of logic programming. As for automated reasoning, we will concentrate on identifying decision problems for the general class of modal logics. To facilitate the presentation, we will thoroughly illustrate the method using straightforward, accessible examples. Methods similar to those used in categorical logic have been used to study modal logic and related deductive systems [1-4], but these previous studies differ from our own approach in several key ways. Unlike our method, for instance, the standard modal logic semantics relies on the accessibility relation between worlds rather than the topological structures in categories. In contrast to our method, also, Priiti and Rau work directly with modal formulas rather than examining their structural composition [5]. Lastly, the method used in this paper differs from the one used in the BIS method in terms of the emphasis placed on the logical framework and the related algebraic and topological characteristics [6]. While the BIS method focuses primarily on finding decision problems for individual modal logics, our presentation will concentrate on identifying decision problems for the general class of modal logics. In the course of our study, we will demonstrate that each individual modal logic has a unique topological structure in categories, thus establishing a general framework for the modal logic as a whole. We will then show that the general framework can be used to prove key properties of modal logic truths and related algebraic and topological characteristics. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI. For web-based model analysis and simulation, please contact the corresponding author at copasi@yield.com.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and solving inverse problems with uncertain input. We introduce an ensemble-based framework that enables the quantification of uncertainty associated with NN-based predictions in a broad range of applications. This framework is subsequently applied to various numerical examples, including function approximation, solving partial differential equations, and solving inverse problems with uncertain input. The results are then compared with alternative uncertainty quantification methods. The proposed framework exhibits greater consistency and is generally more effective than competing approaches. Notably, the proposed framework demonstrates particular success on problems with limited data availability. The proposed framework also effectively identifies nonphysical solutions, indicating that it holds significant potential for addressing real-world problems. Finally, the proposed framework is shown to effectively navigate issues of overfitting even in the absence of regularization. We prove that quantum group analogues of the central embedding principle hold for both compact and non-compact versions, characterized by quasi-split inclusions. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration achieves a contraction rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(e^{-t/\sqrt{d}}\right)$, offering improved convergence compared to policy iteration and inexact policy iteration for $d \geq 2$. Moreover, its computational complexity is significantly lower than that of exact policy iteration for $d \geq 3$. These findings highlight inexact GMRES policy iteration as a highly efficient algorithm for large-scale MDPs with local contraction guarantees. Our analysis also extends to a new class of algorithms, inexact contraction-free policy iteration, along with an example by inexact contraction-free GMRES policy iteration, which exhibits a contraction-free and locally contractible nature with an $\mathcal{O}\left(e^{-t/\sqrt{d}}\right)$ contraction rate for $d \geq 2$. Overall, inexact contraction-free policy iteration presents a valuable approach for MDPs with local contraction-free guarantees. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior. Finally, the study provides insights into the critical exponent, also known as $\alpha$-hyperplane, in the context of $q$-Langton ant walk dynamics on weighted directed trees. These investigations offer novel contributions to the field of q-Langton ant walk dynamics and edge ideals associated with weighted directed graphs. 

Key mathematical concepts employed in this research include analysis of $\alpha$-hyperplanes in q-Langton ant walk dynamics and Kalman-Hillman construction. The theoretical findings can be computationally tested using the q-Langton ant walk dynamics package available on GitHub, which was previously developed by the authors.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate precise rainfall-runoff data. To efficiently handle this expensive objective function, we proposed a two-stage approach utilizing simulated annealing and stochastic gradient descent. The first stage involves generating optimal parameter samples through comprehensive simulations, while the second stage refines the parameters using local optimizations. The results of our experiments reveal that our approach significantly reduces computational costs while yielding superior outcomes compared to other high-efficiency methods. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of the optimal parameter space and developed a time-efficient algorithm to approximate the optimal solution. Validations using both synthetic and real data verified the superiority of our method, revealing that in most cases it achieves at least 50% reduction in computational costs while delivering comparable or improved results. Moreover, we discovered that the optimal parameters we obtained using our method produced satisfactory results when used to solve other related inverse problems. Therefore, we propose that the optimal parameter space generated by our method can be utilized to solve a broad range of related inverse problems, effectively serving as a multi-objective solution. We have named this collective set of optimal parameters the "Hydrological Optimal Parameter Repository (HOPR) database," which can be accessed at https://hydrologicmc.github.io/HOPR/. The proposed approach, along with the associated code and the HOPR database, are freely available at https://github.com/HydroLogicMC/HOPR for the use of researchers and the hydrological community. Farrar et al. (2021) is the initial paper that introduced the approach, while subsequent research included Hernandez and Farrar (2021), a collaborative paper that contributed to the development of the HOPR database with valuable insights. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new learning algorithms that utilize local membership queries to verify the model's accuracy while accounting for example exposure. We propose two decision-making strategies for selecting membership queries that are informed by the model's output, which are accompanied by distributional bound analysis for both binary and multi-category classifications. These new algorithms demonstrate the ability to learn robustly, even in the presence of example exposure, and are empirically verified on simulated data. Our research further explores the application of these models in half-space learning, where we developed two specific algorithms and validated their effectiveness through experimentation. Ultimately, our new membership query selection methods could be utilized to improve the robustness and efficiency of current learning algorithms. Our work also yields the first analysis of concept complexity and its relationship to example exposure, as well as bounds for the natural concept complexity in the presence of random example exposure. Our new bounds are more relaxed than those found in Eufrasio et al. (2019), and are even comparable to the values expected from Valiant (1984) and Kearns et al. (1987) under non-adaptive settings. Our investigation of complex concept bounds for binary classifications also surpasses the values obtained by Gourdeau et al. (2019) and are even comparable to the values expected from Valiant (1984) and Kearns et al. (1987) under non-adaptive settings. Additionally, our natural concept complexity bounds for multi-category classifications outperform the values obtained by Gourdeau et al. (2019) and are even comparable to the values expected from Valiant (1984) and Kearns et al. (1987) under non-adaptive settings. Furthermore, our natural concept complexity bounds for multi-category classifications outperform the values obtained by Gourdeau et al. (2019) and are even comparable to the values expected from Valiant (1984) and Kearns et al. (1987) obtained for non-adaptive settings. Our research also extends the analysis of local membership queries by Gourdeau et al. (2019) while considering example exposure, and achieves tightened bounds that approach information-theoretic limits. Our empirical findings demonstrate the efficacy and robustness of our new algorithms over existing ones on both synthetic and real-world data

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 3 GeV. Jet fragmentation functions remain unchanged when traversing the transverse momentum range of 30-1000 GeV, however, the shape of fragmentation functions differs significantly in the low jet radius when comparing to the standard jet radius. This investigation offers initial insights into jet fragmentation within a heavy nuclear environment. Additionally, the findings provide a groundwork for evaluating quark-gluon equivalence and testing theoretical models of jet interactions within a nuclear environment. Further detailed analysis is feasible due to the impending Run 3 and anticipated Run 4 campaigns at the LHC, anticipating a tenfold increase in recorded data. This research is an initial step towards exploring jet fragmentation within a heavy nuclear environment and sets the ground for future studies to evaluate quark-gluon equivalence and test theoretical models of jet interactions in a nuclear environment, enabled by anticipated increases in recorded data under the conditions of Run 3 and impending Run 4 campaigns at the LHC. The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, each character is classified as a binary option, ignoring the actual character value. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training approach within a Bayesian framework increased the model's robustness and performance. When applied to the current largest dataset, our penultimate model achieved RMSE = 0.4341, 0.2891, and 0.1271 for velocity, velocity dispersion, and flux, respectively. Furthermore, we found that our model effectively isolated intrinsic SN Ia variability from the sample distribution. When compared to existing reduced spectral templates, our model showed improved normalization capabilities and greater coverage of the phase space, yielding 35% and 20% more samples classified as intrinsic for velocities and flux, respectively. Finally, we observed that our model's latent space grouped SNe Ia into three sub-classes, with variable time series patterns distinct from those in the host galaxy's latent space as found in a separate model. Conversely, we noticed substantial overlaps between the intrinsic SN Ia variability and sub-classes in the model's latent space due to rising noise at later epochs combined with limited spectral data. Consequently, further photometric information is required to distinguish between the model's intrinsic SN Ia sub-classes through classification. The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the plume gains mass, as well as the direction in which the particles move within the plume. The studies showed that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the movement of fluid into the plume increases significantly. The rate of fluid movement increased in direct proportion to the ratio of the particles' gain of mass to the fluid's gain of mass, and this increased rate was independent of particle size. In addition, when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are the same, the movement of fluid into the plume decreases slightly. The rate of fluid movement decreased in direct proportion to the particles' gain of mass, and this decreased rate was also independent of particle size. The observations suggest that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the particles hinder the movement of other particles within the plume, creating a condition in which the plume is affected by a "filtering" mechanism. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has at once. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples and the analysis that follows enable the differentiation between inherent disease characteristics and the impact of individual and collective interactions. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for a more nuanced examination of disease spread in networks. For further information, please consult our published paper at arXiv:2106.11049.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persist until the core hydrogen depletion phase, it could impact stellar oscillations, particularly affecting their eigenfunctions and seismic indices. Using the results from recent simulations, we have generated sets of synthetic helioseismology data and used them to conduct a study on the impact of differential rotation and supergranular convection on these measurements. Since these measurements are difficult to replicate in low-Rossby-number stars, we focused on analyzing them for anti-solar cases, where we found that differential rotation has a noticeable effect on seismic indices and velocity flux patterns. Notably, these seismic indices display notable latitude-dependent variations. On the other hand, supergranular convection slightly alters these measurements, primarily by revealing empty convective channels in velocity flux maps. Finally, these anti-solar cases exhibit notable empty channels in the radial and tangential components of the velocity flux, characterized by lower amplitude oscillations compared to the latent phase. By comparing these findings to the initial assumptions, we have determined that seismic constraints on the inner core can be estimated with an error margin of approximately 10%. Further advancements in observational precision and resolution can potentially reduce this error to 5%. Therefore, accurately modeling a star's interior based on seismic data requires convective adjustment at least when the rotation profile exhibits a substantial equator-to-pole gradient. Moreover, we recommend using dynamic models to determine stellar rotation, particularly essential when studying stellar evolution under rotation. By incorporating supergranular convection into these models, we can gain a deeper understanding of a star's interior, but it requires even greater precision and resolution, beyond current seismic limits. large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread

phones enabled by WhatsApp, although personal and immediate, can be exploited to 
circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain. In our study,

India, and Indonesia to investigate the impact of limiting features that contribute 
to rapid information dissemination. Our analysis reveals that current WhatsApp 
restrictions can delay the spread of information but are ultimately insufficient to 
halt the dissemination of highly viral content completely. Consequently, more 
effective measures may be necessary to address the issue of spreading misinformation

the authenticity of messages and promoting fact-based information could be crucial in 
mitigating the spread of baseless rumors and misinformation on WhatsApp. In our 
investigation, we explore two approaches: requiring a phone number linked to an 
identity verifiable by carriers and incorporating a system of trusted news sources 
for fact-based information. Our model indicates that these measures can be highly

biases, highlighting the need for more research in this field. Our study sheds light

research aims to guide the development of more effective strategies for combating

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions. Specifically, our AReLU-based system outperformed existing state-of-the-art techniques, including a system utilizing a more traditional, adaptive activation function, while also yielding more computationally efficient results. Our experimental findings indicate that our AReLU-based system meets the requirements set forth in biometric evaluation criteria, making it a suitable solution for industry implementation. Our source code is freely accessible on GitHub at the provided link. Expanding upon this work, our team recently developed a spoofing countermeasure system for remote voice authentication that incorporates AReLU, which yielded impressive results in an evaluation against the GVvec dataset; this research is documented in a companion paper. Both papers share similar motivations and theoretical foundations. Our approach is also versatile and can be applied to various input types - such as audio features obtained via short-frequency analysis - as evidenced by our ongoing research into the application of AReLU to input data derived from FFT spacing. Our AReLU-based system possesses this adaptability while minimizing computational complexity. Our proposed system is a versatile, efficient, and effective solution for detecting artificial effects within spoken input that arises from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. This research is an extension of our previous work, where we developed a spoofing countermeasure system incorporating attention-based convolutional neural networks and demonstrated improved performance using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset; our current study builds on this success by applying the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) to the convolutional transformation block of our system. Our results indicate that our AReLU-based system yields improved accuracy across multiple input data types and institutional evaluation campaigns, including the DeepASD dataset and DeepASDv2. Our findings also reveal that the adaptive nature of AReLU enables our system to achieve superior performance on challenging tasks, such as distinguishing voice alterations from genuine voice. Our proposed system meets rigorous biometric evaluation criteria, making it a suitable solution for industry implementation and demonstrating enhanced robustness across multiple evaluation campaigns. Our source code is freely accessible on GitHub

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve stable scalars, and eliminating unneeded degrees of freedom.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering the effective theory valid only above a specific energy threshold.  Consequently, the energy density of inflation must be below this threshold for the model to be considered viable. In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be more likely than initially assumed. The trade dynamics between them appears to resemble a version of the prisoner's dilemma, where both types of traders benefit from engaging in a 'cooperative' interaction that maximizes market efficiency. The proposed market model offers a valuable tool for examining the interconnected trades between these two types of traders and could be utilized for other market participants in the future. The findings of this research suggest that the narrative of SRTs preying on CTA profits for financial gain may be an inaccurate one - in fact, the relationship between these traders could be one of mutual benefit. The model proposed in this research is versatile and could be utilized to study the interconnected trade dynamics between a variety of market participants. Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches have been developed for more precise identification. In this research, the mechanisms of dynamic protocol detection in widely used open-source network monitoring tools are examined. Our investigation on HTTP showcases that all evaluated methods are susceptible to evasion tactics, posing significant risks to real-world network surveillance operations. Furthermore, this study reveals that a primary challenge of distinguishing between application protocols remains unresolved in two of the three monitored systems analyzed. To inform operational decisions, this research emphasizes the importance of maintaining protocol definitions, supporting manual configuration, and implementing robust monitoring systems. Additionally, this research highlights the necessity of improved automated detection mechanisms for application layer protocols to ensure effective network security monitoring. Based on these findings, recommendations for enhancing dynamic protocol identification are provided to inform operational decisions. These recommendations emphasize the significance of human oversight, the benefits of manual configuration options, and the need for enhanced training data to improve network surveillance. To address these challenges, this research advocates for the integration of machine learning techniques, the utilization of manual human insights, and the adoption of lead-based monitoring configurations. Finally, this research underscores the value of employing both automated and human-driven analysis in network surveillance to investigate real-world case studies. To address the identified gaps, this research proposes an innovative method utilizing query graphs to analyze HTTP requests. By leveraging the advantages of graph-based monitoring and the ability to incorporate human insights into the analysis, this research demonstrates the feasibility of employing GNNs to identify application protocols. Furthermore, this research showcases the efficacy of the proposed method by highlighting its advantages over existing network monitoring tools in several real-world case studies. To facilitate operational use, this research presents the developed model and associated training data for evaluation in other network surveillance operations. By highlighting the strengths of the method in identifying application protocols, this research emphasizes the importance of integrating human analysis into automated results to enhance network surveillance. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, this research compares the output of the proposed method against known application protocols in three real-world scenarios. To improve operational monitoring, this research recommends integrating the method into existing network surveillance systems and suggests future research directions. Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin ferromagnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this reaction greatly increase the magnon's effective mass, enabling separate regulation of its phase and amplitude via a nearby gate. By manipulating the gate's voltage, we achieved a 100-GHz frequency change and a maximized magnon storage capacity of up to 40 femojoules. The discovery positions magnon-based computing in an optimal position to benefit from the demonstrated integration of superconducting and magnetic components. The innovative concept also yields various practical applications, such as magnon radiosenders generating 50-GHz signals or utilized in magnon-based logic gates with a robust magnon supply. The technique has the potential to improve the efficiency and flexibility of magnon computing and other magnon-based technologies. A significant challenge in various machine learning tasks is overcoming the imbalance of data distribution across different locations. Federated learning offers a solution by allowing a centralized model to be updated across multiple sites, while respecting users' privacy. However, the lack of data in each site hinders the update of the model, especially when users' data distributions differ significantly. This issue can be addressed by leveraging the information shared from users during the federated learning process. In this study, a new perspective on leveraging this shared information is explored through the lens of multivariate Gaussian mixtures. A novel model, called the Gaussian Mixture Model for Federated Learning, is developed to determine the parameters of data distribution and the model itself. This model relies on an asymptotically optimal mixture of Gaussians and uses the EM-algorithm for parameter estimation. Our experimental findings demonstrate that this model significantly outperforms the conventional approach based on naive maximum likelihood in terms of model selection and estimation. Furthermore, our results show that this model can be applied effectively in various scenarios, such as ascertaining whether a user's data is involved in the federated learning process, determining the reliability of a user's local model, and adjusting the federated learning update rule based on users' data distributions. Our study's findings highlight the potential of modeling users' data distributions through mixture of Gaussians as a promising direction for enhancing the federated learning update rule. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Our findings imply that online local news monitoring can provide critical, data-driven insights into social issues and local problems. Furthermore, our work highlights the benefits of increasing diversity in online news datasets, especially those concerning public health crises, by including more outlets and coverage from underrepresented segments of the population. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. We compared its performance with other models, such as a neural network and a decision-making AI, and found that it consistently outperformed them. To study the intricacies of its learning process in detail, we created a simplified, count-based reward system and found that, even with this approach, the AI's performance peaked before it had fully mastered counting. We observed that this over-performing was likely caused by the AI exploiting minor flaws in the training data instead of properly learning the concept of counting. To mitigate this issue, we developed a new reward system that only awarded the AI points for accurately counting more complex scenarios as it progressed, which successfully prevented the AI from rushing to early victories and improved its overall learning efficiency. With these approaches, we were able to simulate the 'give-N' task at a similar scale to the 'learn-N' task and found that both tasks showed similar inflection points in learning and performed relatively equally. To further test the robustness of our findings, we studied the 'pick-N' task - where the AI has to select items from a binary vector - and found that, although it showed a similar inflection point in learning, it consistently outperformed the 'give-N' and 'learn-N' tasks. Through our research, we found that the 'give-N', 'learn-N', and 'pick-N' tasks all have the potential to be used as standards in the automatic assessment of machines' counting abilities. To take our findings to the next level, we created three new rewards systems that challenged the AI to apply its counting abilities in more intricate ways, such as using a combination of binary and ternary vectors, which successfully demonstrated the ability to transfer its learning from one context to another. Ultimately, our research successfully simulated the cognitive milestone of learning to count in machines using the 'give-N'

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients make decisions independently without external guidance. Furthermore, FLVoogd does not necessitate the transmission of sensitive data across the network, as servers only send cluster parameters and clients confine their model adjustments within a defined boundary. Our proposed solution is capable of running on resource-constrained devices and can be viewed as an update to existing distance-controlling testing methods. We strive to address potential challenges and vulnerabilities to establish a framework for distance-controlling testing in FL settings. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images.
The analysis of the dataset revealed that most OCR models generated significant errors when attempting to read new texts.
The competition featured an ensemble challenge where participants combined different Off-The-Shelf (OTS) OCR models to maximize performance using a self-designed metric.
Ultimately, an ensemble of OTS models developed by CRF-Aster, MRCNN, and Segmentation, all trained on the Visual Genome dataset, demonstrated the best results, achieving a 34.08% error rate on the evaluation metric.
The top-performing models were characterized by simple yet effective designs, utilizing pre-trained features and unitary transformations for better feature extraction and data augmentation.
The competition led to proposals for new metrics and evaluation methods to assess the validity of overfitting and data augmentation in scene text recognition.
Additionally, the competition raised questions about the potential limitations of OTS models in extending their capabilities to new texts.

Two main challenges arise when applying CMDP solutions: achieving optimal policies and verifying the feasibility of obtained policies. To overcome these obstacles, researchers present a new algorithm that utilizes a feasibility indicator, enabling effective detection of the closest feasible policy to the optimal one. The method involves transforming the feasibility problem into a dual problem, providing a ascending dynamical programming equation with a suitable Lyapunov function. The results demonstrate that this approach yields a continuous, effective, and computationally efficient method for finding the closest feasible policy. The method also includes a device allocation optimization component that employs a two-stage stochastic programming solution with a globally convergent gradient search algorithm. The feasibility indicator algorithm is then combined with these methods to obtain the closest feasible policy to the optimal. This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective classifier capable of recognizing such a wide range of symbols must be developed. Initially, this study addressed the challenge of segmentation by applying the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering method. Results showed that the accuracy of the designed classifier was 84% for the salient features, while 57% and 53% accuracies were achieved with the pixel and bounding box features respectively. Furthermore, the table-conditional approach outperformed the competing methods by a significant margin. What's more, the integration of the table-conditional approach with the SLIC method increased the overall segmentation accuracy to 90%. Eventually, the combination of the best features and the table-conditional classifier reached an accuracy of 90.5% for the segmentation task. Building upon these findings, a comparable accuracy of 92.5% was achieved for the symbol recognition task with the same features. Consequently, the integration of the table-conditional approach with the SLIC method proved to be highly effective for the segmentation and recognition of handwritten mathematical symbols in an offline setting. What's more, this technique can potentially be applied to other forms of handwritten symbols as well. In conclusion, this research made key advancements in the technology of handwritten mathematical symbols recognition and will likely be applied in the development of mathematical ink-free technology. The source code is available at https://github.com/ashishkml/HMMCS.git for those interested in this field.
