However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily in reducing the gap between the approximated posterior and optimal policy distribution. Furthermore, our approach optimizes exploration within action spaces by targeting areas with higher expected returns. To achieve this, a new leapfrog operator has been developed for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics. Consequently, our approach has shown a significant enhancement in achieved return while reducing safety constraint breaches. Specifically, our results indicate a 14% increase in safe average return and a 20% reduction in safety constraint breaches compared to a straightforward actor-critic model implementation. A thorough theoretical analysis under infinite action space conditions confirms our method's ability to converge towards the optimal policy distribution. Our approach's practical efficacy has been validated through a series of safety-critical reinforcement learning experiments across multiple real-world datasets. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Divergent sensor configurations, including relative positioning, are evaluated for their impact on acoustic flow properties and the effectiveness of the designed controller in achieving stable indoor navigation. This approach shows promise in addressing sensor failure, maintaining safe distance from obstacles, and simplifying the flow modeling of multiple sensors. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we discover that Nereid's spectral data at 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ can be satisfactorily replicated if a portion of its surface is covered by tholins, assuming a low albedo of tholin-covered areas ($\sim$0.03) to account for its low reflectance. Furthermore, comparing our modelled spectra with those of irregularly coloured satellites and bodies, including Phoebe, Nereid, and Ceres, reveals that varying water-ice grain sizes are sufficient to generate their distinct neutral colours. Lastly, examining the spectral variation among these objects may provide insight into the presence of organic materials and/or methane ice. Our study offers a starting point for future analysis of Nereid's spectral characteristics, suggesting that its spectral variation could be attributed to the presence of organic materials and/or methane ice. Additionally, investigating the spectral variation among these objects may provide insight into the presence of organic materials and/or methane ice. Our findings also highlight the need for subsequent observations, emphasizing that Nereid's spectral analysis could be significantly enhanced through high-resolution spectroscopy, which could potentially disclose the presence of organic materials and/or methane ice on this celestial body, as well as those with similar neutral-sloped spectra. If achieved, this could offer valuable insights into the composition of these objects, thereby contributing to the broader field of extraterrestrial spectroscopy. Our analysis supports the notion that Nereid's spectral characteristics hold promise for investigating the properties of distant, icy bodies and their surface features. With advancements in spectrographic technology in the near future, we anticipate that high-resolution spectra of Nereid and similar objects will reveal distinct absorption features, thereby yielding novel information about their compositions, surface features, and water-ice grain sizes. This could potentially provide a deeper understanding of the unique tholin-covered surfaces that distinguish these objects from other icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise this parameter without manual adjustment. By doing so, we develop a reliable Bayesian learning method that adapts optimally to unknown conditions, including sparsely utilised states and limited model knowledge. In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-body excitations are governed by an effective single-particle Hamiltonian based on the non-interacting wave functions of the system. Furthermore, we found a zero-energy excitation characteristic to these bound states with dispersion determined by the minimal quantum metric. Using the framework of topological quantum chemistry, we categorize the bound state spectrum, leading to the identification of Cooper pairs exhibiting Weyl nodes, high angular momentum pairing, and fragile topological features. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line annotations. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution. Ultimately, this study successfully achieves HTR on artificially generated data, utilizing only one sample per symbol. Additionally, the developed generator is utilized to simulate ciphers in the Edward Steichen Cryptogram, a renowned historical document, allowing for a programmatic deciphering approach.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a specific subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it successfully solved the SMMO representative benchmarks at least 2x faster than the Stride-O-Blaze framework and with improved memory localization.  Our research also showed that DynaSOAr's memory allocator is compatible with two popular parallel sorting algorithms, when used in conjunction with the Stride-O-Blaze framework, resulting in a combined speedup of up to 3x over the Erazor allocator and equivalent performance to the KMEANS Particle Cluster (KPC) approach for particle-based sorting with a speedup of 2.5x.  In addition, our research revealed that DynaSOAr's approach is adaptable to various memory patterns, is independent of block structures, and can be scaled to large data sets without performance degradation as the size of the data increased.  Our innovative framework addresses a critical shortage in current research by providing a practical solution for efficient memory allocation and data management in high-performance, object-oriented computing applications for a wide range of algorithms at SIMD scales.  Our contribution also extends to the knowledge area of object-oriented computing by providing a general approach applicable to any SMMO program.  In addition to the scientific contribution, the DynaSOAr framework has practical value as it can be utilized to solve real-world parallel computing challenges for a broad category of algorithms. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. Conversely, the surface slippage regime is influenced by another parameter that takes into account the relationship between surface asperity spacing and the thickness of the complex liquid. Information about the power-law distribution of surface asperity heights is also reflected in the transition between these two parameter spaces. Ultimately, our study offers insights that can be applied beyond foam dynamics to the broader field of complex liquid flow. Additionally, it provides a framework for characterizing surface roughness based on its impact on complex liquid flow behavior. Due to the relative simplicity of our experimental setup, this methodology can be readily adopted by researchers and engineers to assess surface roughness in various applications. Based on our analysis, we recommend two parameters - the Curvature Number and the Spacing Number - to standardize the characterization of surface roughness in terms of its effect on complex liquid flow. These numbers not only facilitate the comparison of different surfaces but also enable the prediction of complex liquid flow behavior on those surfaces. Furthermore, our study's focus on the friction mechanism is expected to foster further discussion and debate in the field of complex liquid dynamics. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 97 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and analyzed the effectiveness of our strategies in handling the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed two new methods for leveraging metadata in classification. Our results demonstrated the significance of incorporating metadata, as well as incorporating a an anomalous class probe to improve accuracy in detecting the outlier class. We attained a state-of-the-art AUC of 95% in using metadata for the outlier class, and achieved a overall AUC of 87% across all classes using our proposed methods. It is worth noting that our code is available on GitHub for reproduction purposes.

Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results indicate the interaction has a negligible impact on the carrier acceleration in sodium at low temperatures. Additionally, our data do not support the idea that the increased mass is solely caused by the interaction of conduction electrons and phonons. Our study also explored the electronic structure of the two-dimensional surface layer in sodium and found that its thickness is approximately two monolayers. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've developed a fundamental expression for work done by macroscopic forces on individual systems, which provides unique insights into the dynamics. This framework enables us to study the work done by each individual force component, referred to as microwork, and we've applied it to the expansion of an ideal gas. The results show that, in the absence of external influence, the work done by each microscopic force is consistently signed, whereas the work done by the dominant pressure force is generally positive, indicating that larger systems are less affected by the forces acting at the molecular level. Additionally, we've used this work done by all individual forces to identify three distinct nonequilibrium phases in the expansion process. These findings are further exemplified through simulations based on a cluster-cluster growth model. The extended application of this model allows us to explore a broader range of nonequilibrium scenarios, including systems that may not be solely composed of ideal gases, such as in the case of gas-sphere and gas-cluster interactions. The approach presented in this study is versatile and can be employed to analyze a variety of nonequilibrium dynamics across a wide spectrum of systems. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce localized waves, thereby confirming previous numerical and experimental observations on the phenomenon in non-precompressed diatomic chains. Nonetheless, an approach grounded in exponential asymptotics fails to accurately predict solitary wave formation for various mass ratios in precompressed diatomic chains. Consequently, these results are contrasted with a numerical study, which indicates that solitary waves can form within a specific mass range but are absent beyond a particular critical value, underscoring the restrictions on the phenomenon reported previously. Moreover, exponential asymptotics fails to effectively predict solitary waves in both precompressed woodpile and diatomic chains when the small parameter is accounted for. Consequently, a shock mitosis event is identified in these solitary waves, resulting in different asymptotic behaviors on opposite sides of the solitary wave. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom. Our detailed examination includes specific examples of the "massless Galileon" and "featureless inflation" models, as well as a massive field during inflation, all of which display notable signals. These models, although inflationary, differ from standard cosmological models, and their characteristics can be identified through upcoming surveys of cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure. Our work lays the groundwork for feature-rich inflation, where the cosmic collider plays a pivotal role in uncovering the underlying physics of these models, and possibly different types of fundamental gravity, by combining low-energy particle physics and cosmology. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we developed the DINO self-supervised method, a form of self-distillation without the need for labelled data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly. Moreover, DINO outperforms other self-supervised methods by a substantial margin, and our method has the added benefit of producing semantic segmentations of superior quality. To facilitate replication, the DINO codebase can be accessed at the specified repository. Further details regarding the method's development, as well as the evaluation results, are presented in the accompanying paper and additional resources. An analysis of the advantages of ViTs over convnets in self-supervised learning also exists in an alternate paper. Additionally, the DINO method has been incorporated into the DeepLearnAMC benchmark, which assesses the performance of self-supervised learning methods using an image classification and semantic segmentation benchmark. As a result, DINO demonstrates robust classification and segmentation capabilities, and functions effectively even when the learning rate is increased to 16, causing the model to converge to our earlier findings. Lastly, the DINO method has been successfully adapted for other ViT architectures, such as ViT-Small and ViT-Large, and has shown promising results on various tasks, including image-level, object-level, and semantic segmentation, in other image datasets. Overall, the DINO method is a versatile and effective tool for self-supervised Vision Transformer learning. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control and creativity. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks and applications, demonstrating its ability to balance consistency and change. The project's code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/visual-lover/Stable-Artist. Additionally, the associated artist's portfolio can be found at https://stablediffusionartist.github.io/. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive models that can be trained using deep neural networks. However, these models are known to yield inaccurate predictions near the boundaries of their training data due to the inherent nature of deep learning. A major challenge lies in differentiating between random uncertainty and biased uncertainty. To address this limitation, we employ Bayesian deep learning and propose an innovative approach that incorporates posterior predictive checks to evaluate the accuracy of predictive models. Our method calculates the probability of predictive errors and adapts the steganographic capacity accordingly. Moreover, we develop an efficient learning algorithm based on maximum-aposteriori that minimizes predictive error while constraining latency. Our experimental results validate the efficacy of our method, showcasing superior performance and increased steganographic capacity compared to conventional methods. For instance, our method achieves a 1.03 bits per channel improvement in steganographic capacity on the Brodatz dataset when set to a 0.01 error threshold. High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear.  This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient.  Researchers developed a novel model, named SMD, comprising three interconnected networks, each mimicking the human visual processing temporarily, permanently, or selectively destroying sensory information.  SMD effectively combines spatial and motion information, outperforming existing action recognition systems in a dataset mimicking human brain activity.  Notably, SMD achieves superior results on a benchmark dataset created from the Cararra dataset, surpassing top-performing action recognition systems by a significant margin.  Additionally, SMD accurately identifies the importance of sensory information for a specific action from large datasets such as Kinetics-600 and HMDB-51. Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where some colors are grouped into sets with size m plus one, it would be true that this graph contains a complete graph with m vertices. This more robust idea has been tested with efficacy for m equals 5 and is now proven to work for all values of m. 

In response to the question of whether this new, robust idea holds true in general, we provide an example of a graph that is assigned colors in the grouped manner but does not contain a complete graph with 4 vertices. This means the robust idea does not always hold, and as a result, it is weaker than Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture, which states that if a graph is assigned t colors, it must contain a complete graph with t vertices. 

However, we also provide an alternative, simplified version of the robust idea. This version says if a graph is assigned t colors in the grouped manner, it must contain a complete graph with t-1 vertices. This version is proven to work and offers the insight that the version with m equals 5 may have been the best possible version of the robust idea. 

Furthermore, we prove that a certain type of graph will always contain a complete graph with an exponentially small number of vertices. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a new explanation for the efficacy of GCNNs in pattern recognition. We analyze the effect of convolutional layers on data nodes in GCNNs, revealing how they shift data features towards pre-defined features over multiple iterations. We further develop a set of essential theorems describing the behavior of GCNNs, supporting the efficacy of the proposed explanation with numerical and visual proofs. We evaluate the new approach using explicit numerical solutions for a simple 2D GCNN, showing that it accurately mirrors the desired network's behavior. We advocate for the proposed approach as a viable method for describing the behavior of GCNNs, offering a clear understanding of these networks' inner workings. We showcase its applicability on a bone age assessment challenge, providing a framework for automatic feature alignment to enhance low-resolution images, ultimately enabling the detection of relevant pattern features. We compare the new approach's performance with that of state-of-the-art deep learning methods, showing its superiority in this specific challenge. We highlight the potential of the proposed approach in enhancing deep learning methods with fundamental mathematical principles, paving the way for the development of new deep learning techniques informed by neural network physics. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this label scarcity by utilizing the parser's own output to improve performance. By integrating two key components - risky prediction avoidance and output refinement - our approach enhances the parser's robustness and accuracy on both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation measures. Experimental results across multiple languages demonstrate significant improvements, averaging 3.2% in F1 score and 0.4 in unlabeled attachment score. Our source code and models are freely available for public use. Firstly, our method encourages the parser to focus on "risky" predictions that are most susceptible to errors to minimize the propagation of mistakes. Concurrently, it employs a refined version of the parser on the augmented dataset to capture better sentence structures. By combining these strategies, our self-training technique yields notable gains, surpassing state-of-the-art results in numerous evaluations. Additionally, our method yields robust performance even when data augmentation is imperfect, showcasing its efficacy under constrained conditions. Ultimately, our approach provides an effective and practical solution to the label scarcity problem, paving the way for the adoption of neural dependency parsing models on small, annotated datasets. From an theoretical standpoint, our method is positioned as a bridge connecting neural models and traditional, rule-based models, utilizing the latter's output as input to the former to achieve improved results. Experimentally, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art results, showcasing its efficacy across multiple languages. Our source code and models are freely available for public use. 

Here are the main contributions of this research:
  1. A novel self-training technique that leverages a refined parser output to improve performance, yielding notable gains in multiple evaluations.
  2. An effective strategy for identifying and mitigating the parser's errors by focusing on "risky" predictions and refining the parser's output.
  3. Notable improvements in F1 score and attachment error rates across multiple languages, averaging 3.2% and 0.4 respectively.
  4. Robust performance when data augmentation is imperfect and an effective means of combining neural models with rule-based models.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (Ptime). In contrast to fixed-point logics, such as Monadic Second-Order Logic (MSO) or Transitive Closure Logic (TCL), CPT facilitates a broad range of operations including recursive function applications and assignments to fresh variables in each step. Our primary aim is to explore the fundamental boundaries of CPT by examining its basic components. Specifically, we investigate under what conditions the CFI-query is CPT-definable on a class of graph and reveal a key distinction in this context. The CFI-query encompasses a range of subproblems, including the Counting Homogeneous Subgraphs Problem (CHSG) and the Existence of a Hierarchy of k-Cliques Problem (kHC), both of which are not solvable by MSO but are CPT-instance of each other, CHSG and kHC. Furthermore, our results show that CPT and MSO have identical decidability boundaries for graph classes, a finding strengthened by the demonstration that CPT and MSO are equivalent on SPT-recursive graph classes, a more refined set of CPT-recursive graph classes. Our analysis also yields a generalized framework for the uniform version of CPT, a approach limited by the dynamic assignment of variables in each step. The proof of CPT's comparative strength with MSO is further exemplified through its demonstration of solvability for the kHC Problem on forest, a problem not resolved by MSO, CRL, or TCL. The approach employed combines a novel application of the fundamental Ackermann trick with a logic tailored to mimic CPT's key operation, the addition of a variable at each step. Our analysis extends Ptime-completeness to a broader category of operations, a concept initially introduced and demonstrated to encompass familiar operations such as matrix multiplication and the shortest paths problem, by showing that CPT is complete for Ptime on forest. Our findings offer key insights into the fundamental power of CPT. Despite this flexibility, systems often exhibit inconsistent behavior, influenced by specific options, arising from the combination of different configurations. In our research, we explore the elimination of system variability to obtain optimal properties, focusing on reduced binary size and improved performance. To achieve this, we eliminate the impact of less important features, reducing the system's dependency on variable parameters, by removing features that do not affect the system's properties. In this paper, we outline our method in detail, illustrating its application with two case studies, also investigating its limitations and raising questions for future investigation. The outcome of this study is a tool, called CMinimizer, allowing users to select the system parameters and obtain an optimized configuration. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the system properties, providing users with valuable insights. Overall, our study demonstrates that feature selection can directly or indirectly influence the system's properties, affecting its size and performance. In particular, our case studies show that disabling certain C pre-processor directives can reduce the system's binary size and improve its speed. In this research, we uncover a novel aspect of software specialization, revealing that removing non-essential features has a direct impact on the system's properties. In conclusion, our study paves the way for future investigations, opening up two main areas of research: (1) optimizing the system's properties through dynamic specialization and (2) evaluating the feasibility of feature selection in close-loop systems. In this realm, we identify feature selection as a promising area of research, with a wealth of opportunities for future investigations. In particular, future researchers can build upon our work, particularly in the domain of dynamic specialization, where current approaches focus on reducing the system's variability without necessarily improving its properties. In contrast, our study demonstrates that reducing the system's variability can directly improve its properties, showcasing the potential of feature selection as a more effective strategy. Furthermore, our research reveals that dynamic specialization and feature selection are complementary techniques, allowing users to obtain the best possible results in specific scenarios. In this context, we highlight the potential of feature selection as a more general and effective approach, applicable to various systems, including those with dynamic behaviors. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion artifact and make ECG signals more readable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach accelerates real-time analysis and diagnosis. Notably, our results demonstrate accurate heart rate variability analysis without the need for signal enhancement. Moreover, successful IBI extraction and HRV metrics are achieved from ECG signals with signal SNR as low as -20dB. We anticipate the proposed architecture to have a significant impact in the field of remote health monitoring using wearable technology. Further discussions on potential applications and future developments are presented. We also provide a comparison with state-of-the-art approaches in signal processing and deep learning to validate our claims. We are confident that our research will contribute to the development of next-generation remote health monitoring and wearable technology systems. We have made our source code publicly available to facilitate future research and innovations. The code can be accessed through our GitHub repository: https://github.com/CompBioMed/Deep-Med-Tiramisu. We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using Legendre-Fenchel transform of the scaled cumulant generating function obtained via a cloning algorithm. Results for the free particle exhibit asymptotically linear behavior on both sides, dependent on a multiplicative factor of the dimension. Conversely, confinement scenarios in two dimensions display distinct behavior when applying active force in either harmonic or anharmonic potentials, each exhibiting varying rate function and mechanism. Moreover, a fluctuation relation for active work distribution is verified in free particles, exhibiting temperature-dependent behavior. Similar verification occurs in cases involving harmonic potential, while in anharmonic cases, verification holds at low active force levels; yet at high levels of active force in anharmonic cases, a distinct effective temperature, derived from the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, is found to govern behavior. These predictions are compared to and validated by direct numerical simulations. benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task

a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our code is available at a repository address.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working on a heat transfer task between a system and a bath with varying temperature. The system's energy is increased via a time-varying force on a particle in a quartic potential. To maximize efficiency in this setup, we developed an optimal protocol that adapts to changing temperatures and energy levels. When given prior notice of temperature fluctuations, we found that the maximum-efficient protocol can be predicted analytically, but otherwise, we relied on numerical solutions. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Our approach starts with solving the equation Du = λu, where D represents the Clifford analysis operator and λ a constant. We then obtain a specific integral expression for Du in terms of u, which subsequently enables the application of the theorem. As a consequence, this methodology also solves the monogenic Cauchy problem under certain constraint. Additionally, we employ the special monogenic functions to establish a extension of the theorem within homogeneous polynomials. Our analysis also yields novel results, including the extension of the theorem to the space of harmonic functions and to the space of rotund harmonic functions. Lastly, we illustrate with several examples the accuracy and simplicity of the obtained estimates.

We identify that these maps exhibit anomalous diffusion due to positive Lyapunov exponents in their invariant measures, which are derived using a random walk approach. We also provide analytical expressions for the scaling variables in the intermixture limits, confirming the results numerically with histogram-based implementations. Additionally, we apply the three-dimensional generalized heterochaos baker map to model a three-jump error process in a complex system, yielding a heavy-tailed distribution of transient lifetimes that can be tailored through parameter adjustment. Since the maps are essentially reinterpreted versions of the Dyson-Brown time model, our findings establish a mathematical equivalence between this model and the heterochaos baker map. Furthermore, we investigate the fractal properties of the maps' invariant sets, which exhibit self-similar structures in their 2D and 3D forms. These set structures provide a physical representation of the maps' ability to encompass the entire space while covering it sparingly, offering a connection to the concept of dimension that is accessible through visual inspection. As a consequence, we propose these sets as viable candidates for investigating the principle of dimension variability in complex systems. This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2021, where experts faced significant challenges in processing complex videos due to dropout and data quality issues affecting feature extraction, leading to rough boundary annotations and deleted video segments. To overcome these obstacles, we employed an ensemble of models, including the BAN and ERNIE models, both initially trained on individual frames and later on aggregated video features. Notably, we explored the potential benefits of providing auxiliary inputs to enhance model performance. While initial experiments on the AQTC dataset yielded subpar results, we achieved a top-1 accuracy of 70.65% on the validation set and 71.09% on the test set with the optimal model. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to make sense of sensory data by balancing the costs of different models, where simpler models offer higher efficiency. However, these models are limited in their ability to explain more complex data. When applied to the study of human face perception, this theory predicts that we should find faces explained by the simplest models possible. Recent research supports this idea, demonstrating that infants and adults respond differently to stimuli consisting of faces and non-face noise. When shown modified faces, adults and infants both react as if the output is noise, indicating that both groups respond as if the output is explained by the simplest models. However, when shown noise, only adults respond as if the output is explained by the simplest models. This difference suggests that humans may possess unique cognitive abilities that influence active inference. Moreover, the findings present a novel explanation for the widespread occurrence of face perception abilities in the animal kingdom. It is proposed that the evolutionary benefit of active inference lies not only in the brain's efficient models, but also in the penalty function that reduces the cost of complex models. Faces may have automatically been linked to a low penalty in the past due to their frequent occurrence and importance in human interactions, resulting in an innate attention boost for objects resembling faces. This mechanism may also contribute to the emergence of face processing abilities in other animals if they encounter the same frequent visual stimuli during their development and evolution. Additionally, it is suggested that active inference plays a key role in the social behaviors of various animals by providing a direct link between cognition and action. This theory's widespread application is then considered, along with the need for further research into its practical uses and limitations. Finally, it is proposed that active inference offers a unique opportunity to integrate cognitive theories with cutting-edge machine learning technologies, allowing for the creation of advanced, biologically grounded artificial intelligence systems. This integration may also yield valuable by-products, such as the development of new image processing algorithms and the advancement of our understanding of human perception. Moreover, it is suggested that the most significant benefit of active inference may lie in its potential to improve our computational methods for generating realistic visual stimuli in artificial intelligence. This could lead to the creation of more lifelike faces and social behaviors in machines, ultimately contributing to the emergence of more sophisticated artificial intelligence systems in the future. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between geographical locations and scheduling parameters under a random policy, eliminating the need for Channel State Information (CSI) after training. Additionally, a novel method is proposed to back-propagate the loss through the network, which enables efficient learning. Experimental results show that the proposed neural network achieves near-optimal performance comparable to the local optimal algorithm with significantly higher computational requirements. This research provides insights into the performance trade-off between data freshness and throughput in wireless D2D communications. Finally, the neural network is shown to be an effective solution for scheduling D2D communications without excessive computational resources. Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Given a time series of graphs, where the presentation of data may vary and sometimes include missing components, detecting events that characterize changes or patterns within these graphs is a challenging problem.  This research aims to develop an effective method to identify events using dynamic graphs through a new model that incorporates both node and edge dynamics.  This model employs a combined approach of the degree-based iterative algorithm and the mean-shift technique to identify events.  This approach recognizes events caused by node activations or changes in subgraphs.  After establishing the model, a theoretical analysis is conducted to prove the model's correctness and consistency.  Experiments with synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy of the method in identifying events compared to existing methods. The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in simulations involving the Navier-Stokes equations in both one-dimensional and three-dimensional settings. This study aims to increase our understanding of accelerating shocks and their behavior, which has significant implications for processes like stellar implosions and supernovae, as well as laboratory astrophysics experiments and inertial confinement fusion. The work also paves the way for generalizing these solutions to more complex situations and exploring their stability using eigenvalue equations and linear stability theory. Finally, the existence of multiple fluid pressure peaks in these solutions is revealed, which has surprising consequences. The findings of this research will be presented in a series of papers and conference talks. In this first report, we will delve into the theoretical framework and one-dimensional simulations. Details about three-dimensional simulations can be found in a companion paper. The pressure-based stability analysis and comparison with other numerical methods will be explored in a subsequent paper. The knowledge gained from this study will be applied to simulate various types of self-similar solutions, including non-similar cases, and even the Rayleigh-Taylor instability in the absence of acceleration. A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial formed by combining the two ellipse equations, allowing for handling all cases of intersection points, including none, one, two, three, or four points. The proposed method has been implemented in C and validated through numerous tests with diverse input ellipses, demonstrating its efficiency for applications involving multiple overlap area calculations in simulations. The determined areas are also utilized to analyze the temporal evolution of overlap areas during collisions. Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rate of work and heat exchanged with the environment can be calculated from the transition probability of these states over time. The fundamental generating functions of these thermodynamic quantities are expressed using path integrals, distinguished by their infinite horizon and vanishing smallness parameters. This study applies non-stationary gauge transformations to these generating functions, confirming the invariance under certain conditions. The transformations have the potential to simplify generating functions for complex systems, making them more tractable to analyze and solve. Specifically, we illustrate the benefit by applying the transformations to an equilibrium motor protein driven by a biochemical reaction, whose analysis was previously hindered by the high dimensionality of its phase space. The transformations have reduced the complexity, enabling us to determine the asymptotic current distribution when the system reaches equilibrium. Moreover, the analytical gauge transformations have revealed the connections between (i) the current distribution, the forward and reverse fluxes, and (ii) the second and third conditional cumulants, all within the context of non-stationary thermodynamics. These relationships have been proven for general Markovian jump processes, even in the absence of gauge invariance. Ultimately, the transformations have expanded the scope of non-stationary gauge transformations to include RG methods, making these techniques applicable to any stochastic thermodynamic system. The technique has been implemented in the software package "NonStationaryGAUGE". A detailed explanation of the methodology, along with the underlying theory and a discussion of the various techniques, is provided in the supplementary material. These variations are likely caused by the planet breaking apart due to a turbulent atmosphere on the host star, rather than another explanation such as a Kuiper belt-like debris shield. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category. Additionally, we apply this framework to investigate the variation of the Milnor fibration over parameter spaces of certain types, including elliptic surfaces and hyperbolic manifolds. Specifically, for hyperbolic manifolds, we demonstrate that the resulting family of fibrations exhibits a discrete, localized structure, and we term this phenomenon a "galloping fibration." Furthermore, we draw parallels with periodic and galloping fibrations to obtain novel topological invariants. Specifically, we derived an expression for the $H_{2k-1}$ homology group of the monodromy $\mathfrak{M}$ of a $k$-dimensional periodic fibration and proposed the conjectural evaluation of the $H_{2k-1}$ homology group of the monodromy $\mathfrak{M}$ of a $k$-dimensional galloping fibration. Lastly, as a case study, we examined the variation of the Milnor fibration for the family of cubic polynomials with Mainardi type periodicity. Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers. Daany can be used for academic purposes at no cost.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical competence. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics. In this context, I propose a revised interpretation of Galileo's impact on science, in which his limitations served as opportunities for others, like Kepler and Hooke, to capitalize on filling mathematical gaps. Ultimately, this analysis aims to highlight that a lack of mathematical skills can still render an individual an effective scientist. Utilizing recent examples from science, I seek to demonstrate that science does not always depend on an in-depth understanding of mathematics in a classical sense. Consequently, the notion of science being inherently mathematical ought to be reevaluated. By redefining what it means to be a mathematician, we may uncover that several scientists were, in fact, competent mathematicians. This discovery could have significant implications, as in the case of Clementine, who in 1693 became the first woman to present original mathematical work to the Royal Society. Her story serves as an exemplary model for women to overcome barriers and contribute to mathematics and science despite persistent obstacles. Even after the Enlightenment, women like Châtelet and Emilie de Châtelet continued to face challenges in their pursuits of science and mathematics. In the 18th century, the perception of Galileo as an inept mathematicician began to affect his legacy, as in the case of d'Alembert's comments, as his experimental methods started to seem inferior to those of Newton, who was seen as the ultimate scientific role model. In the end, the conventional view of Galileo as an innovative scientist continues to persist, as in the case of Kuhn's work, yet this image might be an inaccurate reflection of his true accomplishments. In conclusion, the question of whether science requires mathematics is no longer the primary concern, as the real challenge lies in recognizing the contributions of individuals who, like Galileo, occupy gray areas between mathematics and science. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our research utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable PIC regions required within the MHD domain to achieve such convergence. Nonetheless, the MHD-AEPIC model remains the most cost-effective method, offering a substantial computational advantage. Therefore, this new model provides a practical solution for exploring the intricate kinetic aspects of magnetic reconnection via adaptive embedding of PIC models into meaningful, fluid-based MHD simulations. This approach can be applied to a broad spectrum of collisionless reconnection phenomena, including interactions between two magnetic flux ropes, cartoon reconnection layers, and interactive reconnection in various configurations. The model can further be generalized to investigate the coherent growth of spiral structures via the incorporation of initial conditions representing two magnetic islands. Lastly, the model has the potential to be used in the investigation of the growth of magnetic bubbles, a physical phenomenon characterized by the emergence of ion holes and the presence of electron-scale turbulence. Here, the application of PIC models is crucial in accurately modeling this associated electron dynamics. Therefore, adapting PIC models into relevant sections of MHD simulations of magnetic reconnection can provide a comprehensive understanding of this reconnection process. The model can be extended to various reconnection scenarios, such as the growth of magnetic islands, by embedding PIC models into MHD simulations of a reconnection layer. This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons and project discussions handled by the software engineer.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of handling complex tasks on their own and make strategic decisions in collaboration with their human counterparts.  Ultimately, the productive collaboration between these experts yields innovative computing systems and the discovery of the underlying cognitive processes that govern human thought and behavior.  This course draws inspiration from the groundbreaking Systems Neuroscience work in the 1980s at the Caltech, the pioneering work in the field of Artificial General Intelligence by the Cognitive Science department at the Caltech, and the recent breakthroughs in the systems neuroscience field at the MIT.  The course is designed to meet the following objectives:  (i) to review existing knowledge and provide a summary of the most relevant research in the systems neuroscience and artificial general intelligence domains; (ii) to apply this summary to the development of intelligent systems capable of making strategic decisions; and (iii) to use computational models to investigate the interconnected brain functions that govern human thought and behavior.  The course is composed of seven chapters that cover the following topics and are available online at the url:  https://stanford.io/2RC6z8F.  Chapter one sets the course objective and provides an overview, while chapter two and three provide an in-depth analysis of the systems neuroscience and the general intelligence solutions, respectively.  Chapter four and five focus on the intelligent digital assistants that learn from their expert counterparts, while chapter six delves into the cognitive processes that govern human thought and behavior.  Finally, in chapter seven, the course concludes and provides recommendations for the ongoing research in this domain.  The url provided includes additional resources such as the complete course videos and slides that are available to the public for the duration of one year.  The course received an evaluation through the course evaluations platform, and the feedback results showed an overwhelmingly positive response from the course participants.  The course was composed of the following key components - 18 hours of the instruction time, 70 hours of the discussion time, and 70 hours of the homework time.
